== compares values by calling __eq__. is compares identity, whether two names point at the same object. Use is only for singletons such as None. a == b can be true while a is b is false.

The trap: small integers and some strings are cached by CPython, so a is b can appear to work in a test and then fail on other values. Never use is for numbers or strings.

85. Write an idempotent extractor for a paginated REST API with rate limits.

The shape interviewers expect:

import random, time, requests

def fetch_all(url, params, max_retries=6):
    cursor = load_checkpoint()                 # resume where the last run stopped
    while True:
        for attempt in range(max_retries):
            resp = requests.get(url, params={**params, "cursor": cursor}, timeout=30)
            if resp.status_code == 429 or resp.status_code >= 500:
                wait = float(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt))
                time.sleep(wait + random.uniform(0, 1))   # backoff with jitter
                continue
            resp.raise_for_status()                       # other 4xx: fail loudly
            break
        else:
            raise RuntimeError("retries exhausted")
        page = resp.json()
        write_page(page["items"])          # upsert on a natural key, not append
        cursor = page.get("next_cursor")
        save_checkpoint(cursor)            # only after the page is stored
        if not cursor:
            return

What makes it idempotent: records are upserted on a key, and the checkpoint moves only after a page is written, so a crash re-fetches at most one page and re-applying it changes nothing.

The traps: retrying on every 4xx (a 401 will never succeed), backing off without jitter (all workers retry at the same instant), and offset-based pagination over data that changes during the run, which skips or repeats rows. Prefer cursor-based pagination when the API offers it.

86. A plain Python UDF makes a PySpark job ten times slower. Why, and what are the alternatives?

A Python UDF runs in a separate Python worker process next to each executor. Rows are serialized from the JVM to Python and the results back again, one row at a time, and Catalyst cannot see inside the function to optimize or push filters through it.

The options, best first:

  • Built-in functions (F.when, F.regexp_extract, F.transform) stay in the JVM and are optimized.
  • A pandas UDF (@pandas_udf) moves data in Arrow batches and runs vectorized pandas code, which removes most of the per-row cost.
  • A Scala or Java UDF registered in the JVM avoids the Python boundary entirely.

The trap: a pandas UDF still crosses a process boundary. When a built-in function exists, it beats any UDF.

87. Validate incoming records in Python before loading them.

Declare the schema once and validate at the boundary. A dataclass with type hints documents the shape but does not check it at runtime. A validation library such as Pydantic does:

from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class Order(BaseModel):
    order_id: str
    amount: Decimal
    ordered_at: datetime

good, bad = [], []
for raw in records:
    try:
        good.append(Order(**raw))
    except ValidationError as e:
        bad.append({"raw": raw, "error": str(e)})   # quarantine, do not drop

Bad records go to a quarantine table with the error, so the load continues and someone can fix and replay them. Alert when the quarantine rate crosses a threshold. Silently dropping rows is what produces question 60’s missing 10,000.

Java

Java comes up in rounds for teams that run Spark, Kafka, Flink or Hadoop on the JVM, and in banks such as American Express that run a separate fundamentals round.

88. How does HashMap work internally, and what changed in Java 8?

A HashMap is an array of buckets. put(k, v) computes k.hashCode(), mixes the high bits into the low bits, and uses hash & (capacity - 1) as the bucket index. Capacity is always a power of two. Entries that land in the same bucket form a linked list, and equals() finds the right one.

When the number of entries passes capacity * loadFactor (default load factor 0.75, default capacity 16), the table doubles and entries are redistributed.

Since Java 8, a bucket whose list grows past 8 entries is converted to a red-black tree, provided the table has at least 64 buckets. That turns the worst case for a heavily colliding bucket from O(n) to O(log n).

The follow-up: HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent writes can lose entries or corrupt the structure. Use ConcurrentHashMap (next question).

89. HashMap vs Hashtable vs Collections.synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap.
  • HashMap: not synchronized; allows one null key and null values.
  • Hashtable: a legacy class; every method is synchronized on the whole table; no null keys or values.
  • Collections.synchronizedMap(map): a wrapper that locks one mutex around every call. Iteration still needs a manual synchronized block.
  • ConcurrentHashMap: since Java 8, it uses CAS to insert into an empty bucket and locks only the first node of a bucket otherwise, so writers to different buckets do not block each other. Reads do not lock. Iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException. No null keys or values.

The trap: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is a race even on a ConcurrentHashMap, because two threads can both pass the check. Use the atomic putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent or merge.

90. JVM memory areas and garbage collection, and how they show up in a Spark executor.
  • Heap: objects. It is split into a young generation (new objects, collected often) and an old generation (long-lived objects).
  • Metaspace: class metadata, in native memory since Java 8, replacing PermGen.
  • Thread stacks: one per thread, holding frames and local variables. Deep recursion gives StackOverflowError.
  • Direct and native memory: off-heap buffers used by Netty, Arrow and Spark’s off-heap mode.

G1 has been the default collector since Java 9. It splits the heap into regions and collects the ones with the most garbage first, against a pause target.

In Spark, a long GC pause shows up as high “GC Time” for a task in the UI, and in the worst case as an executor lost after missed heartbeats. A container killed by YARN or Kubernetes for exceeding its memory limit is usually off-heap growth, which is what spark.executor.memoryOverhead covers. More heap does not fix it. See question 33.

91. The equals() and hashCode() contract, and what happens when a key is mutated.

If a.equals(b) is true, a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). The reverse is not required. Overriding equals without hashCode breaks every hash-based collection: two equal keys land in different buckets, so get misses and a HashSet holds duplicates.

If a field used in hashCode changes after the object is inserted into a HashMap, the entry stays in the old bucket. get with the same object then looks in the new bucket and returns null, and the entry leaks. Make keys immutable. Java record types and Scala case classes generate a consistent equals and hashCode from immutable fields.

92. volatile vs synchronized vs AtomicLong.
  • volatile guarantees visibility: a write by one thread is seen by later reads in other threads, and it is not reordered. It does not make count++ atomic, because that is a read, an add and a write.
  • synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility for a block. It is correct, and it serializes the threads.
  • AtomicLong and the other atomics use compare-and-swap to make single-variable updates such as incrementAndGet() atomic without a lock. Under heavy contention, LongAdder spreads updates across cells and is faster for counters.

The classic use of volatile is a stop flag read by a worker loop. The classic bug is a volatile int counter that loses increments.

93. Why does Spark throw "Task not serializable", and how do you fix it?

org.apache.spark.SparkException: Task not serializable means a closure sent to the executors refers to an object that does not implement Serializable. The most common case: a lambda inside a class uses a field or method of that class, so the whole enclosing instance is captured, together with its non-serializable members (a database connection, a logger, the SparkContext).

Fixes:

  • Copy the needed field into a local variable before the lambda, so only that value is captured.
  • Mark members that should not travel as transient, and create them lazily on the executor.
  • Create per-partition resources, such as a connection, inside mapPartitions or foreachPartition, not on the driver.
  • Make small helper classes Serializable, or use static methods or a Scala object.

The stack trace’s “Serialization stack” lists the exact chain of fields that pulled the object in. Read it from the bottom.

94. Java Streams: lazy evaluation, and when parallelStream() is a bad idea.

Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) build a pipeline and run nothing. A terminal operation (collect, count, forEach) pulls elements through it, fused into one pass. This is the same idea as Spark’s transformations and actions (question 21), inside one JVM.

parallelStream() splits the work across the common ForkJoinPool. It hurts when the source splits badly (a LinkedList, or I/O), when the per-element work is tiny, when the lambda has side effects on shared state, or inside a server where every request shares the same pool. Inside a Spark task it competes with Spark’s own task threads for the executor’s cores.

Scala

95. What does a case class give you, and why does Spark use them?

A case class generates equals, hashCode and toString from its constructor fields, a companion apply (no new needed), copy with named arguments, and unapply for pattern matching. Its fields are vals, so instances are immutable by default.

Spark derives an Encoder for a case class, so ds.as[Order] gives a typed Dataset[Order] with compile-time field checks, while the data stays in Spark’s binary row format.

The trap: a typed lambda such as ds.filter(_.amount > 100) is opaque to Catalyst, so the filter is not pushed to the Parquet reader. The column expression ds.filter($"amount" > 100) is pushed down. Use typed lambdas where type safety matters more than pushdown.

96. val vs var vs lazy val vs def.
  • val: evaluated once, at definition, and cannot be reassigned.
  • var: mutable. Avoid it in shared or Spark code.
  • lazy val: evaluated once, on first access, and then cached. Thread-safe initialization has a small locking cost.
  • def: re-evaluated on every call.

A lazy val inside a Scala object is a common way to create one expensive resource per executor JVM, such as a client or a connection pool, without serializing it from the driver (see question 93).

97. Option vs null, and map vs flatMap vs a for-comprehension.

Option[T] is Some(value) or None, so absence is part of the type and the compiler makes the caller handle it. Option(x) turns a Java null into None.

map transforms the value inside. flatMap is for functions that themselves return an Option, so you get Option[B] instead of Option[Option[B]]. A for-comprehension is syntax for a chain of flatMap calls and a final map:

for {
  user  <- findUser(id)          // Option[User]
  email <- user.email            // Option[String]
} yield email.toLowerCase        // Option[String]

The trap: opt.get on None throws NoSuchElementException. Use getOrElse, fold or pattern matching.

98. Implicits in Scala 2 and given/using in Scala 3: what are they, and where does Spark rely on them?

An implicit parameter is filled in by the compiler from values marked implicit in scope. An implicit conversion or an implicit class adds methods to an existing type. Scala 3 splits these uses apart: given instances and using parameters for context, and extension methods for added syntax.

Spark depends on implicits through import spark.implicits._. That import provides the Encoder instances behind toDF(), toDS() and as[T], and the $"col" string interpolator.

The version detail: Spark 3.5 is built for Scala 2.12 and 2.13, and Spark 4 for Scala 2.13 only. Spark does not publish Scala 3 builds, so Spark code still uses Scala 2 implicits. The forgotten-import error is Unable to find encoder for type.

99. Trait vs abstract class.

A class can mix in several traits but extend only one class. Traits are how Scala composes behaviour: logging, retry, metrics. In Scala 2, a trait cannot take constructor parameters; Scala 3 allows them. An abstract class can take constructor parameters and is easier to call from Java.

Use a trait for a capability that mixes into many types. Use an abstract class for a base type that needs constructor arguments, or Java interop. Mention linearization when several traits override the same method: the rightmost trait in the mix-in order wins, and super calls go right to left.

100. Write a tail-recursive function, and say what @tailrec guarantees. 
import scala.annotation.tailrec

def sum(xs: List[Long]): Long = {
  @tailrec
  def loop(rest: List[Long], acc: Long): Long = rest match {
    case Nil    => acc
    case h :: t => loop(t, acc + h)       // the recursive call is the last action
  }
  loop(xs, 0L)
}

A call in tail position is compiled into a loop, so the stack does not grow. @tailrec does not create the optimization. It makes the compiler fail if the call is not in tail position, so a later edit cannot silently bring back a StackOverflowError. In practice, foldLeft does the same job in one line.

Data modeling

These build on questions 51 to 54. The data modeling guide covers each topic in depth with runnable examples.

101. Model a sales fact for five sales channels and three product hierarchies. What is the grain?

Declare the grain first: one row per order line, the lowest level the source records. Channel becomes a dim_channel foreign key, not five separate fact tables, so cross-channel totals are a plain GROUP BY.

Product hierarchies (category, brand, merchandising group) are attributes of dim_product, or separate hierarchy tables if they are ragged or change independently. The fact holds only the product key. A hierarchy is a property of the product, not of the sale.

If one channel records data at a coarser level (wholesale reports daily totals, not lines), do not mix that into the line-level fact. Build a second fact at the daily grain, and conform the shared dimensions so the two can be compared.

102. Role-playing, junk and degenerate dimensions.
  • Role-playing dimension: one physical dimension used in several roles. An order fact has order_date_key, ship_date_key and delivery_date_key, all pointing at dim_date, usually exposed as three views named for the role.
  • Junk dimension: a small dimension that combines low-cardinality flags and indicators (is_gift, payment_type, promo_flag) into one row per combination, so the fact holds one key instead of many flag columns.
  • Degenerate dimension: a dimension key with no dimension table, such as order_number stored on the fact. It is used for grouping lines into an order and for tracing back to the source.
103. What are conformed dimensions, and what is a bus matrix?

A conformed dimension has the same keys, attribute names and meanings in every fact that uses it. dim_customer in sales and in support tickets then gives results that can be compared, and “drilling across” both facts by customer segment is valid.

The bus matrix is the planning grid: business processes as rows (orders, shipments, returns), shared dimensions as columns (date, customer, product), and a mark where a process uses a dimension. It shows which dimensions must be conformed before teams build facts separately. Without one, each team builds its own customer dimension and the numbers stop agreeing.

104. SCD Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 6: how do you choose?

Ask how the business reports history:

  • Type 1 when only the current value matters, or the change is a correction. History is restated.
  • Type 2 when facts must report under the value valid at the time, for example sales by the region the customer was in when they bought.
  • Type 6 when users need both “as was” and “as is” on the same row: Type 2 version rows, plus a current-value column overwritten on every version, so no extra join is needed for current reporting.

The choice is per attribute, not per table. email can be Type 1 while loyalty_tier is Type 2 in the same dimension. Question 51 covers the MERGE implementation.

105. A fact arrives before its dimension row (an early-arriving fact). What do you load?

Never drop the fact and never load a NULL key. Two standard options:

  • Unknown member. Point the fact at a reserved key such as -1 (“Unknown”). Reprocess the fact when the dimension arrives.
  • Inferred member. Insert a placeholder dimension row with the business key and default attributes, flagged is_inferred = true. When the real row arrives, overwrite the placeholder in place (a Type 1 update, even for a Type 2 dimension), so the fact’s key stays valid.

The inferred member avoids reprocessing facts, and is the more common answer. Monitor the count of inferred rows that never get completed.

106. One big table (OBT) vs a star schema in a lakehouse.

An OBT pre-joins the fact with its dimension attributes into one wide table. Columnar formats read only the columns a query needs, and compression handles the repeated values well, so wide tables are cheaper than they were in a row store. Dashboards get simple, join-free SQL.

What an OBT costs: a Type 1 dimension change means rewriting every fact row that carries the attribute; history semantics are fixed when the table is built; and every new attribute is a backfill.

A defensible answer keeps the star as the source of truth and derives OBTs for specific dashboards. The OBT can then be rebuilt from the star at any time.

System design

Expect one system design round at most product companies. The 2026 guides describe it as the round that carries the most weight. The follow-ups are predictable: why this storage layer, what you ruled out, how backfill works, what breaks when a source changes, and what it costs over time.

107. Design a pipeline that ingests 1 TB of clickstream a day and serves dashboards at under 2 seconds P95.

Start with the numbers. 1 TB a day is about 12 MB/s on average, so plan for 3 to 5 times that at peak. Then go layer by layer:

 SDK / web ──► Kafka (partition by user_id) ──► stream job ──► bronze table
                                                     │          (append, raw)
                                                     ▼
                                    silver: deduplicated, sessionized events
                                                     │
                                                     ▼
              gold: pre-aggregated by minute/hour × dimension ──► serving store
                                                                  (OLAP engine)

The key decision is that the dashboards do not scan raw events. Two seconds at P95 comes from pre-aggregated gold tables, or from a real-time OLAP store such as Druid, Pinot or ClickHouse, not from a lake query over a terabyte.

Cover deduplication by event ID, late events with a watermark, a schema registry for the event contract, partitioning by event date, and compaction of the small files from streaming writes (question 36).

The follow-ups: how many Kafka partitions (from peak throughput per partition and consumer parallelism), and how you replay a day after a bug (re-read bronze, not Kafka, once retention has passed).

108. Backfill nine months of history after a logic fix, without double counting and without stopping the daily job.
  • Make every run partition-scoped and overwrite-based. Each run replaces one date partition (INSERT OVERWRITE, Delta replaceWhere, Iceberg dynamic overwrite). A backfill is then many runs of the normal job with old dates, and reruns are safe.
  • Write to a shadow table or branch first. Backfill into a copy (or an Iceberg branch), reconcile row counts and totals against the old output, then swap atomically.
  • Throttle it. Run in date batches with limited concurrency, so the backfill does not starve the daily SLA. Run the newest months first if consumers care most about them.
  • Freeze the inputs. Read from a snapshot or bronze, not from a source that is still changing.

The trap: appending recomputed data on top of the old output. That is the double count.

109. An upstream API changes a field from a string to an object, and the pipeline starts failing. What do you do in the next hour?

In order:

  1. Stop the damage. Pause the job, or let it fail closed. Do not let it write partial or mis-parsed data into tables consumers read.
  2. Keep the raw data. Make sure bronze is still landing the raw payloads, so nothing is lost while you fix the parser.
  3. Tell people. Post to the consumer channel: which tables are stale, since when, and the next update time.
  4. Fix forward. Parse both shapes, mapping the old string to the new object’s field, and route anything unparseable to quarantine.
  5. Replay from bronze for the affected window, then verify counts.

Afterwards: a schema contract with the producer, a schema check at ingestion that alerts before the transform fails, and a test with the new payload. Question 59 covers schema evolution in general.

110. Design CDC replication from a PostgreSQL OLTP database into a lakehouse table. 
 PostgreSQL WAL ──► Debezium (logical replication slot) ──► Kafka topic per table
                                                                 │
          initial snapshot ─────────────────────────────────────┤
                                                                 ▼
                         Spark / Flink: order by LSN per key, MERGE into table

Points to cover:

  • Initial snapshot plus stream. Take a consistent snapshot, then apply changes from the log position where the snapshot ended.
  • Ordering. Apply changes per primary key in log order (LSN), and keep the latest LSN on the target row, so a replayed or late event older than the stored one is ignored.
  • Deletes. Apply them as deletes or soft-delete flags. Handle the tombstone records Kafka uses for compaction.
  • Operational risk. A replication slot that nobody consumes keeps WAL on the primary until the disk fills. Monitor slot lag.

The data modeling guide runs an idempotent CDC apply end to end.

111. Estimate storage and cost at one, three and ten years for a 500 GB-a-day source.

Interviewers want arithmetic, stated assumptions and the levers that change it:

  • Raw: 500 GB a day × 365 ≈ 180 TB a year.
  • As compressed Parquet at an assumed 5:1 ratio: about 36 TB a year, so about 110 TB at three years and 360 TB at ten, before copies.
  • Multiply by the layers you keep (bronze, silver, gold) and by time travel or snapshot retention, which keeps old files alive.

Then the levers: lifecycle rules that move old bronze to colder storage classes, a retention policy per layer, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup, and aggregating old detail when nobody queries it. Compute usually costs more than storage, so mention the incremental processing that avoids recomputing history every day.

State the compression ratio as an assumption to be measured on a sample. Real ratios depend on the data.

112. Design an event deduplication layer for at-least-once delivery at billions of events a day.

At-least-once delivery means duplicates are normal, so deduplication is a design component, not a cleanup job.

  • Key. Use a producer-assigned event ID. Without one, hash the business fields, and accept that identical genuine events will merge.
  • Window. In streaming, keep the seen IDs in state with a TTL or watermark (dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark in Spark 3.5), sized to the longest realistic redelivery delay.
  • Sink. Make the write idempotent too: MERGE on the event ID, or a primary key in the serving store, which catches duplicates that arrive after the state has expired.
  • Measure. Track the duplicate rate. A sudden rise usually means a producer retry storm, not more traffic.

Questions 38 and 39 cover exactly-once for payments and Kafka.

Orchestration and Airflow

113. How do you make an Airflow DAG idempotent?

Each task run must process a fixed, well-defined slice of data and produce the same output however many times it runs.

  • Use the data interval, not the clock. Read data_interval_start and data_interval_end from the context (or `` in templates) instead of calling datetime.now(). A rerun of last Tuesday then processes last Tuesday.
  • Overwrite the slice the task owns (a date partition), or MERGE on a key. Never append.
  • Keep tasks atomic. Write to staging and swap, so a failed task leaves nothing half-written for the retry to trip over.

The trap: a task that “loads everything since the last run” using a watermark stored outside Airflow. A manual rerun of an old interval then loads the wrong data.

114. catchup, backfill, and what happens when you deploy a DAG with a start_date in the past.

With catchup=True, the scheduler creates a run for every interval between start_date and now that has not run yet. Deploying a daily DAG with a start_date a year ago creates 365 runs at once. With catchup=False, only the latest interval runs. Set it explicitly on every DAG: the default comes from catchup_by_default, which Airflow 3 changed from True to False, so the same DAG behaves differently after an upgrade.

Control it with max_active_runs, pools and task concurrency, and run deliberate backfills with the backfill command, so history is reprocessed in a throttled way. Airflow 3 runs backfills through the scheduler, where earlier versions ran them in a separate CLI process.

The trap: catchup on a DAG that is not idempotent (question 113). Every catch-up run then loads the same “latest” data.

115. Sensors: poke vs reschedule vs deferrable, and why sensors can deadlock a cluster.
  • Poke mode holds a worker slot for the sensor’s whole wait, checking on an interval.
  • Reschedule mode releases the slot between checks and is rescheduled for the next one.
  • Deferrable operators hand the wait to the triggerer process, which watches many waits asynchronously, and use no worker slot at all until the condition fires.

If many poke-mode sensors wait on files that arrive late, they can occupy every worker slot, and the tasks that would produce those files cannot start. Use deferrable sensors for long waits, set a timeout, and decide what a timeout means: fail and alert, or skip. Question 74 covers the “upstream data has not arrived” scenario.

116. What is XCom for, and what should you never put in it?

XCom passes small values between tasks: a file path, a row count, a batch ID. Values are stored in the metadata database by default.

Do not pass datasets through XCom. Large values bloat the metadata database and slow the scheduler and UI. Write the data to object storage or a table and pass its location. If you need large XComs, a custom XCom backend can store the payload in object storage and keep only a reference in the database.

117. What changed in Airflow 3, and what does an interviewer expect you to know about it?

Airflow 3.0 was released in April 2025. The changes that come up:

  • Assets replace Datasets as the name for data-aware scheduling: a DAG can run when an upstream asset is updated, not only on a timetable.
  • DAG versioning: the UI shows which version of a DAG’s code each run used.
  • Task SDK and execution API: tasks talk to the scheduler through an API instead of connecting to the metadata database directly, which is what makes remote and multi-language execution possible.
  • Removals: SubDAGs, SLA callbacks and the execution_date context key are gone. Use TaskGroups, deadline alerts or external monitoring, and dag_run.logical_date.

Also mention dynamic task mapping (.expand(), from Airflow 2.3): it creates one task instance per input at runtime, for example one per file.

Warehouses: Snowflake and dbt

118. What is a Snowflake micro-partition, and how does clustering affect query performance?

Snowflake stores each table as micro-partitions: immutable, columnar units of 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, created automatically in load order. For every micro-partition it keeps metadata, including each column’s min and max values.

A query with a filter skips the micro-partitions whose range cannot match. That is pruning, and it is the main performance lever. Pruning works only if the data is laid out so that ranges do not overlap much. Data loaded in date order prunes well on date and badly on customer_id.

A clustering key (ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (col)) has Automatic Clustering rewrite micro-partitions in the background to reduce overlap. It costs credits, so use it only on large tables with a dominant filter. Check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION before and after.

119. Permanent vs transient vs temporary tables in Snowflake.
  • Permanent: Time Travel (1 day by default, up to 90 on Enterprise edition) plus a 7-day Fail-safe period.
  • Transient: persists until dropped, Time Travel of 0 or 1 day, and no Fail-safe.
  • Temporary: exists only for the session, Time Travel of 0 or 1 day, no Fail-safe.

Use transient tables for staging and intermediate data that can be rebuilt. Fail-safe storage is billed, so a frequently rewritten permanent staging table pays for seven days of old versions nobody will restore.

120. Snowflake streams vs tasks.

A stream is change tracking on a table: it records the inserts, updates and deletes since its offset, exposed with METADATA$ACTION and METADATA$ISUPDATE columns. Consuming the stream in a DML statement advances the offset when the transaction commits.

A task is scheduled SQL: a cron schedule or interval, optionally chained into a graph of tasks, and optionally conditioned on SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('stream_name'), so it runs only when there are changes.

Together they give incremental ELT inside Snowflake: the stream says what changed, and the task merges it into the target on a schedule.

121. A Snowflake virtual warehouse is expensive. How do you tell whether it is the right size?

Look at the query history and profiles before changing the size:

  • Spilling to local or remote storage in the query profile means the warehouse is too small for those queries. Scale up.
  • Queuing (queued time in query history) with short queries means too much concurrency. Scale out with a multi-cluster warehouse, rather than up.
  • Low utilization, with a warehouse running between sparse queries, means auto-suspend is too long. Lower it, because billing is per second with a 60-second minimum each time it resumes.
  • Poor pruning (partitions scanned close to partitions total) means the query or the layout is the problem, and no size fixes it.

Separate workloads (ELT, BI, ad hoc) onto separate warehouses, so each can be sized and attributed, and set resource monitors as a spend backstop.

122. dbt incremental models: how do they work, and what goes wrong?

An incremental model builds the full table on the first run. On later runs is_incremental() is true, and the model selects only new or changed rows:

{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id',
          incremental_strategy='merge') }}

SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
WHERE updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM {{ this }})
{% endif %}

With a unique_key and the merge strategy, changed rows update in place instead of duplicating. The strategies available (append, merge, delete+insert, insert_overwrite) depend on the adapter.

What goes wrong: late-arriving rows with an updated_at older than the current max are skipped forever, so subtract a lookback window. A model logic change does not fix history until you run with --full-refresh. And without a unique_key, every rerun appends duplicates.

123. dbt snapshots and dbt tests.

A snapshot implements SCD Type 2 on a source table. Each run compares the current rows with the stored versions, using the timestamp strategy (an updated_at column) or the check strategy (a list of columns), and closes changed versions with dbt_valid_to while inserting new ones with dbt_valid_from. Snapshots only see the state at run time, so changes between two runs are lost. CDC catches every change; a snapshot catches only the state at each run.

Tests are assertions run as queries. The generic ones are unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships (referential integrity). Singular tests are SQL files that should return zero rows. Put unique and not_null on every model’s grain key, which is the cheapest protection against the fan-out in question 81. Model contracts can also enforce column names and types at build time.

Data quality and observability

124. What do you monitor on a production table, and where do the alerts go?

Five signals cover most incidents:

  • Freshness: the last successful load time against the SLA.
  • Volume: the row count against its usual range for that day of the week.
  • Schema: added, removed or retyped columns.
  • Distribution: null rate, distinct counts and value ranges on key columns.
  • Lineage: which upstream tables feed it, so a failure can be traced to its source and its downstream impact listed.

Alerts go to the team that owns the table, with the table name, the failed check, the expected and actual values, and a runbook link. Route by severity: a page only for broken SLAs on critical tables, a channel message for the rest. An alert nobody acts on should be deleted or fixed, because alert fatigue hides the real one.

125. What is the write-audit-publish (WAP) pattern?

Write new data somewhere consumers cannot see it, audit it with quality checks, and publish it atomically only if the checks pass.

In Iceberg, write to a branch (or stage a snapshot with spark.wap.id), run the checks against the branch, then fast-forward main to it. In Delta, or in any table format, write to a staging table and swap or MERGE after the checks pass. dbt’s equivalent is building into a separate schema and swapping it in.

Failed data never reaches a dashboard, and the failed batch stays available for debugging. The cost is extra latency and the storage for the staged data.

126. A producer team wants to rename a column you consume. How does a data contract handle it?

A data contract is an agreed, versioned specification of a dataset: the schema, the meaning of each field, the quality guarantees, the SLA and the owner. It is enforced in CI for the producer, so a breaking change fails their build before it reaches you.

A rename is a breaking change. The contract process is to add the new column, keep publishing the old one (deprecated) for an agreed period, tell consumers, and then remove the old column in a new major version. Question 59 covers the consumer side.

LLM and AI data pipelines

These are newer. They appear in 2026 interview guides for teams that feed models or run LLM calls inside pipelines.

127. Design a pipeline that processes 10,000 documents a day through an LLM, within rate limits, retries and a cost budget.

Treat the LLM as a slow, rate-limited, metered external API:

  • Queue the work. Put document IDs on a queue, and have a pool of workers sized to the provider’s request and token limits, not to the document count.
  • Back off on 429 and 5xx, with jitter and a retry cap (question 85). Send documents that keep failing to a dead-letter queue.
  • Make it idempotent and cached. Key results by document ID plus content hash plus prompt version, so a retry or rerun does not pay twice, and only changed documents are reprocessed.
  • Budget explicitly. Estimate tokens per document, track spend per run, and stop or degrade (a smaller model, a summary first) when the daily budget is reached.
  • Validate the output. Parse it against a schema and quarantine invalid responses, as in question 87.

Store the prompt version and model ID with each result, so outputs can be traced and regenerated when either changes.

128. Keep a vector index in sync with a source table of documents.

This is CDC again, with an embedding step:

  • Detect changes with a change feed or a content hash per document, and re-embed only new or changed documents.
  • Chunk deterministically, with chunk IDs derived from the document ID and position, so a re-embed replaces the old chunks instead of adding to them.
  • Propagate deletes. A document deleted at the source must be deleted from the index, or retrieval keeps returning it. This is the case most often forgotten.
  • Version the embedding model. A new model needs a full re-embed into a new index, then a cutover, because vectors from two models cannot be compared.

How to prepare from this list

Start with the frequency table. Window functions, skew, idempotency, late data and incremental loads appear at most companies. Being solid on those five covers most rounds.

Prepare by company type. For product companies, practise designing systems out loud and coding without an IDE. For services and consulting firms, know Azure Data Factory and Databricks operationally, implement SCD Type 2 from memory, and prepare the managerial stories.

Answer scenarios with evidence. For every “it became slow” or “the numbers are wrong” question, the structure is the same: what changed, where you look, what you found, what you fixed, and how you verified it. That structure is what these interviews reward.

Then drill by component. Once the company-tagged questions are solid, use the component section to cover the rounds your target companies run: Java or Scala for JVM-heavy teams, Snowflake and dbt for analytics-engineering roles, and system design for every senior role.

Do not memorise answers. Interviewers change one condition (“now the key is null”, “now there is no timestamp”) and watch whether the answer adapts. Every outline above names the mechanism so you can reason from it.

Use it to drill one round at a time. Every technical question has a collapsed answer outline: the mechanism, the trap and the follow-up you should expect. Click a question to open it. A list of “questions asked at company X” is only useful if it tells you what the interviewer is testing. Most of the posts these questions came from do not: they give a question title and move on, and the same thirty titles repeat under a different company name every week. This post does the merging. It takes the questions from public LinkedIn interview-experience posts for data engineer roles, removes duplicates and near-duplicates, rewrites each one as a precise question, and groups them by the skill they test. Each technical question then gets an outline of what a strong answer covers, written the way the Spark interview questions post does it: the mechanism first, then the trap. How the questions were collected The source set is public LinkedIn posts from October 2026 that describe a data engineer interview at a named company, found through LinkedIn content search for “data engineer interview experience” and “interview experience PySpark SQL round”. Only posts that listed concrete questions were kept. Posts that described a process without questions, and posts for other roles (UX designer, GenAI engineer), were dropped. Three things about this source are worth knowing before you use it: The company attribution is weak. One twelve-question banking list appears word for word under Wipro, American Express and Databricks. One American Express post appears from four different accounts, one PayPal post from three, and one Cognizant post from three. Many of the posting accounts sell interview kits. Read a company label as “this question set circulated with this name on it”, not as a transcript. The questions are still representative. The same question reaching you from five accounts says nothing about one company, but it says a lot about the market. The frequency counts below are the most reliable signal in the set. Compensation figures were left out. The posts quote CTC ranges, but none can be checked, and they are not what you prepare against. public posts ──► keep posts that list questions ──► normalise wording │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ merge duplicates and near-duplicates ──► tag each question with │ the companies it came from ▼ group by skill ──► outline what a strong answer covers What each company focuses on The table summarises the reported rounds for each company and the question that best captures what it tests. Duplicates, retries, late data and schema change make up most of the scenario questions, and they are all versions of one question: what happens to the data when something goes wrong. SQL Each question lists the companies it was reported under in brackets. 1. Find the Nth highest salary, overall and per department, using more than one approach. [PwC, PayPal, Atlassian, IBM, Infosys, TCS, Capgemini, HCA Healthcare] Expect to give three approaches and say when each one breaks. DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) = N is the default. It treats ties correctly, so the “second highest” is the second distinct value. A correlated subquery, WHERE N - 1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary AND e2.dept = e1.dept), works without window functions. It is quadratic per group, so say so. ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 over SELECT DISTINCT salary is fine for the overall case and awkward per department. The trap: ROW_NUMBER() returns a wrong answer when two people share the top salary, because it gives them ranks 1 and 2. The “without RANK or a subquery” variant (TCS, IBM) wants a self-join: MAX(e1.salary) where a strictly greater e2.salary exists. 2. ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK, and when can a ROW_NUMBER solution be rewritten with DENSE_RANK? [PwC, EY, Walmart, Atlassian, Capgemini, IBM] For the values 100, 100, 90: Function Result Use it for ROW_NUMBER() 1, 2, 3 Exactly one row per group (deduplication, latest record) RANK() 1, 1, 3 Competition ranking with gaps DENSE_RANK() 1, 1, 2 Nth distinct value They agree only when the ORDER BY key is unique within the partition. Once there are ties, a DENSE_RANK() = 1 filter returns several rows per group where ROW_NUMBER() = 1 returns one. The follow-up is determinism. ROW_NUMBER() over a non-unique sort key picks an arbitrary row among the ties, and in Spark that choice can change between runs. Add a tiebreaker column. 3. Find duplicate records, delete them, and keep only the latest record per business key. [PwC, EY, Microsoft, PayPal, Tiger Analytics, Ford, HCA Healthcare] Find: GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Keep the latest: SELECT * FROM ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY business_key ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingest_id DESC) AS rn FROM src) t WHERE rn = 1; Delete in place depends on the engine. In SQL Server, a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() and DELETE ... WHERE rn > 1 works. In Delta or Iceberg, write the deduplicated result with MERGE or INSERT OVERWRITE rather than issuing row-by-row deletes. The follow-up: an exact duplicate (every column equal) and a key duplicate (same key, different values) are different problems. The first is a DISTINCT. The second needs a rule for which version wins, and that rule belongs to the business, not to you. 4. Running totals: claim amount per policy, account balance per transaction, sales per day. [Coforge, Wipro, American Express, Databricks, Microsoft, PayPal, Atlassian] SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY txn_ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). State the frame explicitly. With an ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. That includes every peer row with the same txn_ts, so two transactions in the same second both show the combined total. ROWS gives a true row-by-row balance. For a balance, debits must be negative before the sum. Say that you would check the sign convention in the source. 5. Consecutive patterns: orders on consecutive days, usage rising three months in a row, a value appearing three times in a row. [Walmart, Comcast, American Express] Two standard techniques: LAG/LEAD comparison. For “three rising months”, compare usage with LAG(usage, 1) and LAG(usage, 2) in the same row. Gaps and islands. date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user ORDER BY date) is constant across a run of consecutive dates. Group by that difference and keep groups with COUNT(*) >= k. Gaps and islands generalises to any run length. LAG needs one comparison per step. Deduplicate dates first: two orders on the same day break the ROW_NUMBER() arithmetic. 6. Anti-joins: customers who ordered in January but not February at 100M rows, customers with no transaction in 90 days, LEFT SEMI vs LEFT ANTI, and missing records without a LEFT JOIN. [Cognizant, Wipro, American Express, EPAM] NOT EXISTS or a LEFT ANTI JOIN is the correct shape. NOT IN is the trap: if the subquery returns a single NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never true and the query returns zero rows. LEFT SEMI JOIN returns left rows that have a match, with no right-hand columns and no duplication when the right side has several matches. LEFT ANTI JOIN returns left rows with no match. At 100M rows in Spark, both are hash or sort-merge joins on the key. Prune the right side to distinct keys for February before the join, and partition by month so January and February are each a single scan. EXCEPT on the key columns also works, at the cost of a full deduplication. 7. Second most recent login for every user, or the penultimate order for every customer. [PwC, Capgemini] ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_ts DESC) = 2. Expect the follow-up: what about a user with only one login? This query drops them. If the requirement is “one row per user, null when there is no second”, left join the result back to the distinct users. 8. Traverse a hierarchy (employees to managers, components to leaf parts) with a recursive CTE. [Microsoft, American Express] WITH RECURSIVE chain AS ( SELECT emp_id, manager_id, 1 AS depth FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.emp_id, e.manager_id, c.depth + 1 FROM emp e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.emp_id) SELECT * FROM chain; Name the two failure modes: a cycle in the data recurses forever, so cap the depth or track visited ids, and the recursion cost grows with depth. Leaf nodes are rows whose id never appears as a parent: an anti-join on manager_id. Spark 3.5 does not support WITH RECURSIVE. There, the usual answer is an iterative self-join loop in the driver that stops when an iteration adds no new rows. 9. List currently active accounts from an accounts table and a status-audit table, where accounts with no audit record count as active. [HDFC Bank] Take the latest audit row per account with ROW_NUMBER(), left join it to accounts, and keep rows where COALESCE(latest_status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'. The test is whether you notice that an inner join silently drops accounts that were never audited, which is the “count as active” clause. 10. Top 3 salaries per department, or top 3 products per region. [KPMG, Microsoft, Infosys] DENSE_RANK() <= 3 if ties should all be returned, ROW_NUMBER() <= 3 if exactly three rows are required. Ask which. In PySpark the same logic is Window.partitionBy("region").orderBy(F.desc("sales")) with F.dense_rank(). 11. A query that ran in 2 minutes now takes 20, or a query over billions of rows with several large joins needs optimising. [EY, Walmart, Comcast, PwC, KPMG, PayPal, EPAM, Ford] Work from evidence, in this order: Compare the plans. Get the execution plan now and, if possible, from when it was fast. A changed join strategy or a lost index or partition filter explains most regressions. Check what changed. Data volume, statistics (stale statistics lead to bad join orders), a new predicate that stopped partition pruning, a function wrapped around a filter column. Reduce the bytes read. Partition and cluster on filter columns, select only needed columns, push filters below joins. Fix the joins. Pre-aggregate before joining, filter early, broadcast the small side, check for row explosion from many-to-many keys. The “it used to be fast” framing is deliberate. The interviewer wants to hear that you start with the plan diff, not with adding indexes. 12. NULL semantics: in aggregates, joins and filters, and what happens with a = null, b = null, a == b? [Comcast, PayPal, Tiger Analytics, KPMG] Comparison: NULL = NULL is NULL, not true, so a filter drops the row. Use IS NULL, Spark’s null-safe <=>, or eqNullSafe in PySpark. Joins: null keys never match in an equi-join. Two rows with a null customer_id do not join to each other. Aggregates: COUNT(col) and AVG(col) skip nulls, while COUNT(*) counts every row. An average that “drops” rows is usually this. Grouping: GROUP BY puts all nulls into one group. 13. SQL fundamentals asked as quick checks: CTE vs subquery, GROUP BY vs HAVING, TRUNCATE vs DELETE, indexing, materialized views. [KPMG, Tiger Analytics, PayPal, Capgemini] Pair The answer in one line CTE vs subquery Same plan in most engines; a CTE is readable and can be referenced twice, but is not automatically materialised WHERE vs HAVING WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after TRUNCATE vs DELETE TRUNCATE deallocates all data with minimal logging and no WHERE; DELETE removes rows and can be filtered Index A sorted structure that turns a scan into a seek; costs write throughput and storage Materialized view A stored query result, refreshed on a schedule or incrementally; trades freshness for read cost On a lakehouse, the index question usually becomes partitioning, clustering and file-level statistics, because Parquet tables have no B-tree indexes. 14. Find customers whose purchases in the last 90 days exceed their average monthly purchase by more than 50%. [Deloitte] Two aggregates at different grains, joined on customer: total over the last 90 days, and average of monthly totals over a baseline period. Then filter on recent_90d > 1.5 * avg_month * 3, or compare per-month rates. The question is testing whether you define the baseline before writing SQL. “Average monthly purchase” over which months, and including months with zero purchases? Months with no rows do not exist in a GROUP BY, so the average is overstated unless you generate a month calendar. Python and coding These rounds are about clean, correct code under pressure, not about algorithms rarely seen in data engineering. 15. Data-shaped Python: deduplicate a list keeping order, count frequencies, find duplicate employees by ID, group consecutive numbers into ranges. [PwC, EY, Azure-role interviews] Order-preserving dedupe: list(dict.fromkeys(items)), since dicts keep insertion order. A seen set with a loop is the explicit version. Frequency: collections.Counter(items). Duplicates by key: group into a defaultdict(list) keyed by ID, keep groups with more than one record. Consecutive ranges: sort, then start a new range whenever x != prev + 1. State the complexity for each: all are O(n) after the O(n log n) sort in the last case. 16. Classic algorithm questions: merge overlapping intervals, longest substring without repeating characters, longest consecutive sequence, first non-repeating character, pairs summing to a target, top K frequent elements. [Atlassian, PwC, Walmart, PayPal, Tiger Analytics] Problem Approach Complexity Merge intervals Sort by start, extend the last interval while overlapping O(n log n) Longest substring without repeats Sliding window with last-seen index map O(n) Longest consecutive sequence Set; start counting only from x where x-1 is absent O(n) First non-repeating character Counter, then one pass in original order O(n) Pairs summing to target Hash set of complements O(n) Top K frequent Counter plus heapq.nlargest, or bucket sort O(n log k) For “first non-repeating element in a stream” (PayPal), the follow-up is memory: an ordered dict of candidates plus a set of seen-twice values. 17. Flatten nested JSON, process a multi-GB CSV without loading it into memory, and compute top routes by revenue without pandas. [Coforge, Microsoft, Tiger Analytics, PwC, KPMG] Nested JSON: a recursive function that joins parent keys with a separator, and turns lists into either indexed keys or exploded rows. Decide which with the interviewer, because it changes the row count. Large CSV: stream with csv.reader line by line, or pandas.read_csv(chunksize=...), keeping only aggregates in memory. For anything that needs a sort or join, say you would hand it to Spark or DuckDB. Top routes without pandas: a defaultdict(float) of route to revenue, then heapq.nlargest(3, ...). 18. Python language questions: decorators, multithreading vs multiprocessing, mutable vs immutable objects, exceptions. [American Express, Data QA interviews] Decorator: a function that takes a function and returns a wrapped one; use functools.wraps to keep the name and docstring. A retry or timing decorator is a good example to give. Threads vs processes: CPython’s GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so threads help I/O-bound work and processes help CPU-bound work. Mutability: lists, dicts and sets are mutable; tuples, strings and frozensets are not. The classic bug is a mutable default argument shared across calls. Spark architecture and execution 19. What happens, end to end, when a Spark application is submitted? [Grab, Azure-role interviews] spark-submit launches the driver, which creates the SparkSession. The driver asks the cluster manager (YARN, Kubernetes, standalone) for executors. Code builds a logical plan; nothing runs until an action. On an action, Catalyst analyses and optimises the plan and picks a physical plan. The DAG scheduler cuts the plan into stages at shuffle boundaries. The task scheduler sends one task per partition per stage to executors. Shuffle files are written at each stage boundary and read by the next stage. Results go back to the driver or are written to storage. The follow-up is always “where does it break?”: driver memory on collect(), executors at shuffle, and the cluster manager when resources are not granted. 20. Given a sequence (read CSV, repartition(2), filter, select, groupBy, collect), say how many jobs, stages and tasks Spark creates. [Azure-role interviews] Work it from the shuffles. repartition(2) is one exchange and groupBy is another, so the action produces three stages: the scan stage (one task per input split), a stage of 2 tasks after the repartition, and the post-aggregation stage with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions tasks (200 by default), which AQE may coalesce to fewer. Reading a CSV with schema inference adds its own job before any of this, because Spark has to read the file to infer the types. That extra job is the detail the question is designed to catch. 21. Narrow vs wide transformations, transformations vs actions, and lazy evaluation. [Capgemini, Azure-role interviews, HCA Healthcare] A narrow transformation (filter, select, withColumn) computes each output partition from one input partition. A wide one (groupBy, join, distinct, repartition) needs data from many, which forces a shuffle and a stage boundary. Transformations only add to the plan; actions (collect, count, write) trigger execution. Laziness is what lets Catalyst push filters into the scan and collapse projections before anything runs. 22. RDD vs DataFrame vs Dataset, and SparkContext vs SparkSession. [HCA Healthcare, American Express, Azure-role interviews] RDDs are opaque objects that Spark cannot optimise. DataFrames carry a schema, so Catalyst can prune columns and push filters, and Tungsten stores rows in a compact binary format. A Dataset is a typed DataFrame in Scala and Java; in Python only the DataFrame exists. SparkSession (since 2.0) is the entry point for SQL, DataFrames and the catalog. It wraps a SparkContext, which is the lower-level connection to the cluster. 23. What is the Catalyst optimizer, and what is predicate pushdown? [Grab, Comcast, Azure-role interviews] Catalyst turns a query into a parsed plan, resolves it against the catalog (analysed plan), applies rule-based rewrites (optimised logical plan), then picks a physical plan with strategies and cost estimates. Whole-stage code generation then compiles parts of the physical plan to JVM bytecode. Predicate pushdown moves filters as close to the data as possible: into the Parquet reader, where row-group min/max statistics skip data, or into a JDBC source’s WHERE clause. Show it with df.explain(): PushedFilters in the scan node. 24. How does Spark decide the number of partitions, and what is a good target partition size? [Comcast, Azure-role interviews] File scans: splits are bounded by spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes, 128 MB by default, adjusted by openCostInBytes so many small files are packed together. File count does not set partition count directly. Shuffles: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, 200 by default, which AQE coalesces toward spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes (64 MB). Explicit: repartition(n) and coalesce(n). A useful target is 100 to 200 MB of input per task. Too small means scheduling overhead dominates; too large means spills and long tasks. Partitioning, shuffle and joins 25. repartition() vs coalesce() vs repartitionByRange(): what happens internally and when to use each. [EY, Walmart, Infosys, American Express, HDFC Bank, TCS, Azure-role interviews] Operation Shuffle Result repartition(n, cols) Full Even, hash-partitioned partitions coalesce(n) None Merges partitions on the same executor; can be uneven repartitionByRange(n, cols) Full, after sampling Sorted ranges; good before writing sorted output The trap: coalesce(1) before a write does not just produce one file. With no shuffle to separate them, it pulls the upstream stage down to one task, so the whole computation runs single-threaded. repartition(1) keeps upstream parallelism and pays for one shuffle instead. 26. How does a broadcast join work, when do you avoid it, and what if neither side is small? [American Express, HCLTech, EPAM, Netflix, Azure-role interviews] The driver collects the small side, builds a hash relation and sends it to every executor, so the large side joins locally with no shuffle. Spark picks it automatically below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB by default), or when you add a broadcast() hint. Avoid it when the “small” side is large after decompression, because it must fit in driver memory and in every executor. A forced hint on a wrong size estimate is a common source of driver OOM. When neither side is small: filter and project both sides first, pre-aggregate if possible, bucket both tables on the join key to avoid the shuffle on repeated joins, and let AQE switch strategy at runtime once actual sizes are known. 27. Broadcasting vs bucketing, and partitioning vs bucketing. [KPMG, Azure-role interviews] Partitioning splits a table into directories by column value, which lets queries skip directories. It suits low-cardinality filter columns like date. Bucketing hashes a column into a fixed number of files per partition. Two tables bucketed the same way on the join key can sort-merge join with no shuffle. It suits high-cardinality join keys. Broadcasting is a per-query choice for one small table. Bucketing is a layout choice paid once at write time for repeated large joins. 28. What are bloom filters, and how do they speed up joins? [American Express] A bloom filter is a compact bit array that answers “definitely not present” or “possibly present”. Built from the join keys of the smaller side, it lets the larger side drop rows that cannot match before the shuffle. Spark added a runtime bloom-filter join optimisation in 3.3, controlled by spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.enabled. Parquet and Delta also use bloom filters on columns, for point lookups on high-cardinality fields that min/max statistics cannot prune. 29. Joining two large datasets runs out of memory. What do you do? [KPMG, Netflix, Azure-role interviews] Find where it fails before changing anything. An executor OOM during a sort-merge join is usually skew: one key’s rows do not fit in one task. A driver OOM is usually a broadcast that was too large. Then: remove a forced broadcast hint, filter and project before the join, check for a many-to-many key that multiplies rows, handle skew (AQE or salting), and raise shuffle partitions so each task holds less. Increasing executor memory is the last step, not the first. Data skew 30. How do you identify data skew in the Spark UI? One task runs 45 minutes while the rest finish in 3. [Netflix, Comcast, Azure-role interviews] In the stage’s task table, compare the max with the median for duration, shuffle read size and records. A max many times the median, on a stage that follows a shuffle, is skew. Spill on that one task confirms it. Then find the key: df.groupBy(key).count().orderBy(desc("count")) usually shows one value, often a null or a default like 0 or UNKNOWN. 31. Fix skew: AQE skew join, salting, and what to do when AQE is disabled or one key holds 60% of the rows. [HCLTech, Coforge, American Express, HDFC Bank, PwC, Ford, HCA Healthcare] AQE skew join (on by default since Spark 3.2) splits a shuffle partition that is both 5 times the median (skewedPartitionFactor) and larger than 256 MB (skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes) into smaller pieces, and replicates the matching partition from the other side. It only acts on sort-merge joins, and only above those thresholds. Salting by hand: add a random salt 0..N-1 to the skewed side’s key, explode the other side’s matching rows N times with the same salt range, join on (key, salt), then aggregate. Choosing N (HDFC asked this directly): roughly the hot key’s size divided by the target partition size. Too small leaves the hot partition hot; too large multiplies the other side by N for no benefit. When one key is 60% of the data, check whether that key should be joined at all. If it is a null or placeholder, filter it out and union it back after the join. That is often the whole fix. Memory and caching 32. cache() vs persist(): default storage levels, what happens when cached data does not fit, and how to release it. [HCLTech, Cognizant, Azure-role interviews] cache() is persist() with the default level. For a DataFrame the default is memory and disk (PySpark shows it as MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER); for an RDD it is MEMORY_ONLY. persist(level) lets you choose. When it does not fit: with a memory-and-disk level, evicted blocks spill to local disk; with memory only, they are dropped and recomputed from lineage when next needed. Cached storage competes with execution memory in the unified pool, so caching too much slows shuffles. Release with unpersist(). The follow-up: caching is lazy, so nothing is stored until an action runs over the cached DataFrame. 33. Spark memory management, driver vs executor memory, and why a job hits OOM despite enough cluster resources. [American Express, Netflix, Azure-role interviews] Executor heap minus 300 MB reserved is split by spark.memory.fraction (0.6) into a unified pool shared by execution (shuffles, joins, sorts) and storage (cache). Execution can evict storage; storage cannot evict execution below spark.memory.storageFraction. Off-heap overhead (spark.executor.memoryOverhead) covers JVM internals, Python workers and network buffers. OOM with ample cluster capacity is a per-task problem: one skewed partition, an oversized broadcast, collect() on the driver, or Python UDF workers exceeding overhead, which shows up as a container killed by YARN or Kubernetes rather than a Java heap error. Performance and troubleshooting 34. A job that took 2 hours now takes 8 (or 3x or 4x longer). Walk through the investigation. [Wipro, Deloitte, TCS, Databricks, EY, Azure-role interviews] What changed? Input volume, code, cluster, configs, upstream schema. Most regressions are a change nobody announced. Compare the Spark UI for a good and a bad run, stage by stage. Find the stage whose time grew. In that stage, check input size, shuffle size, spill, task time distribution (skew), GC time and failed or retried tasks. Check the storage layer: small files accumulating, a partition filter that stopped pruning, a table growing without compaction. Fix the cause and verify on comparable data. Interviewers listen for a hypothesis tested against evidence, not a list of tuning parameters. 35. A Spark job or streaming query gets slower over days or weeks. What do you look at? [Azure-role interviews, Netflix] Things that grow without bound: the number of small files in the input table, streaming state size (no watermark, so state is never dropped), the checkpoint or metadata log, Delta or Iceberg metadata without maintenance, and an ever-growing lookup table that was once small enough to broadcast. 36. Too many small files: in a PySpark job, a streaming pipeline, or 50 billion files in an S3 lake. [Amazon, Comcast, Grab, HCLTech, Netflix] Prevent: repartition by the table’s partition columns before writing, use optimised or auto-compacting writes, and give streaming triggers a sensible interval so each micro-batch writes fewer, larger files. Repair: run compaction (OPTIMIZE in Delta, rewrite_data_files in Iceberg, clustering in Hudi) partition by partition. Table formats commit the rewrite atomically, so readers see old or new files and never a mix. That is how you get “no downtime”. At 50 billion files, add that listing itself is the bottleneck. Moving to a table format replaces directory listing with a metadata scan, and compaction then runs in batches ordered by query value. 37. How do you size a cluster for 100 GB, optimise a 500 GB CSV, or cut Spark cost while holding the SLA? [Azure-role interviews, TCS, American Express, Cognizant] Size from partitions: 100 GB at about 128 MB per task is roughly 800 tasks. A few waves of those across executors with 4 to 5 cores each sets the cluster size. Then check shuffle volume, which is often larger than input. For a 500 GB CSV: give an explicit schema (inference reads the data twice), make sure the file is splittable (gzip is not), and convert to Parquet once if it will be read again. For cost: autoscaling, spot or preemptible workers for stateless stages, file compaction so fewer tasks run, and removing unnecessary caching. Measure cost per run before and after. Streaming and Kafka 38. How do you achieve exactly-once processing for payment events? [Paytm, Atlassian, Netflix] Exactly-once is an end-to-end property, not a setting. In Structured Streaming it needs a replayable source (Kafka offsets), checkpointed progress, and an idempotent or transactional sink. Spark’s own Kafka sink is at-least-once, so writing back to Kafka needs downstream deduplication. In practice: write to a Delta, Iceberg or Hudi table, whose commits are tied to the batch ID, or MERGE on the event ID. On the producer side, Kafka’s idempotent producer and transactions stop duplicates entering the topic. 39. Duplicate events in Kafka or a streaming job writing duplicates to Delta: how do you prevent and resolve them? [Paytm, Databricks, Netflix] dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark (Spark 3.5+) or dropDuplicates on the event ID plus event time with a watermark, so state is bounded. Then make the write idempotent: MERGE on the event ID inside foreachBatch, or Delta’s txnAppId and txnVersion options so a replayed batch is skipped. To repair existing duplicates, rewrite the affected partitions with a ROW_NUMBER() dedupe. 40. Event time vs processing time, out-of-order and late events, and watermarks. [Comcast, Paytm, Amazon, Netflix] Event time is when it happened; processing time is when Spark saw it. Window aggregations should use event time, or a delayed batch puts events in the wrong window. A watermark (withWatermark("event_ts", "2 hours")) tells Spark how late data may arrive. State older than the watermark is dropped, and events later than it are discarded. For Amazon’s version (“30% of events arrive 45 minutes late”): either widen the watermark past 45 minutes and pay for the state, or keep a tight watermark for the real-time view and correct with a batch job that re-aggregates late data into the affected windows. 41. Checkpointing in Structured Streaming: what is in it, and what happens if the checkpoint directory is deleted? [HCLTech, Comcast] The checkpoint holds the offset log (what each batch will read), the commit log (which batches completed) and the state store for stateful operators. Restart reads it to resume exactly where the query stopped. Delete it and the query starts as new: offsets come from startingOffsets, so you reprocess or skip data, and all aggregation state is lost. Duplicates in a non-idempotent sink are the usual result. 42. Kafka consumer lag keeps growing, or a streaming job falls behind at peak. How do you troubleshoot? [Paytm, Netflix, Databricks] Compare input rate with processing rate in the streaming query progress. If processing is slower: check for skew across Kafka partitions, too few partitions for the consumers, slow sinks, and state growth. Spark reads at most one task per Kafka partition unless minPartitions splits them. Fixes: more topic partitions, maxOffsetsPerTrigger to bound batch size, a cheaper sink path, and scaling executors. A lag graph that grows steadily means capacity; a sawtooth means slow batches. 43. Batch vs micro-batch vs continuous streaming, and how to choose batch or streaming. [Databricks, Ford, PayPal, Tiger Analytics, Atlassian] Micro-batch (the Structured Streaming default) runs small batches with second-level latency and exactly-once with a suitable sink. Continuous processing targets millisecond latency, but supports only map-like operations with at-least-once guarantees, and is rarely used. Choose streaming when the consumer acts on data within minutes. Otherwise a scheduled batch is cheaper and easier to backfill. Many teams run streaming with availableNow triggers to get streaming semantics at batch cost. 44. Find users who viewed the same product three times in one hour without purchasing. [Amazon] Aggregate views by (user, product) over a one-hour event-time window, keep counts of three or more, and anti-join against purchases for the same (user, product) and window. In streaming, a watermark bounds the state. Clarify “one hour”: tumbling windows miss three views that straddle a boundary, so a sliding window or a session-style range check is the honest answer. Lakehouse and table formats 45. How does Delta Lake provide ACID transactions and handle concurrent reads and writes without locks? [Databricks, PwC, Infosys, Cognizant] Every change is a new JSON commit file in _delta_log, numbered in sequence. A table version is the result of replaying commits, with Parquet checkpoints every so often to keep that fast. Readers pick a version and read exactly its files, so they never see a partial write. Writers use optimistic concurrency: they write data files, then try to create the next commit file atomically. If another writer took that version first, Delta checks whether the two touched conflicting files, and either retries or fails with a ConcurrentModificationException subclass. 46. Time travel, OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and Z-ordering in Delta. [Databricks, KPMG, Capgemini] Time travel: VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF reads an old version, for audits, reproducing a report or undoing a bad write with RESTORE. OPTIMIZE: compacts small files into larger ones. Z-order: OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (col) co-locates values so file-level statistics skip more files on filters. VACUUM: deletes files no longer referenced by any version within the retention period, 7 days by default. The trap: VACUUM below the retention period removes the files time travel needs, and can break long-running readers. 47. A Delta table has grown to several terabytes and reads are slow. Why, and how do you fix it? [Databricks, EPAM] Check in this order: small files (count files per partition), filters that do not match the partitioning or clustering, stale or missing column statistics, a long transaction log without recent checkpoints, and wide rows read in full. Fixes are compaction, clustering or Z-ordering on the common filter columns, selecting fewer columns, and moving partitioning off high-cardinality columns. 48. Delete individual rows in Delta without rewriting whole files, and how data skipping differs from SQL indexes. [HCLTech] Deletion vectors mark deleted rows in a small sidecar file, so a DELETE touches only metadata, and the rewrite happens later during compaction. Without them, Delta rewrites every file containing a deleted row (copy-on-write). Data skipping uses per-file min/max statistics in the transaction log to skip whole files. Unlike a B-tree index it does not locate individual rows; it only works when values are clustered across files, which is why it pairs with Z-ordering. 49. Delta Lake vs Hudi vs Iceberg, and Parquet vs ORC vs Avro. [Goldman Sachs] Delta Lake Apache Hudi Apache Iceberg Metadata Ordered JSON log with checkpoints Timeline of instants Snapshot, manifest list, manifests Strength Spark and Databricks integration Upserts, record-level index, incremental pulls Engine neutrality, hidden partitioning, partition evolution Row updates Copy-on-write or deletion vectors Copy-on-write or merge-on-read Copy-on-write or delete files Parquet and ORC are columnar and suit analytics. Avro is row-based with an embedded schema and suits streaming and record exchange. The format choice is about the workload, not a ranking. The open table formats comparison goes further. 50. Auto Loader vs COPY INTO, Medallion architecture, and Unity Catalog. [Coforge, Databricks, EPAM, Capgemini, HCA Healthcare] COPY INTO is an idempotent SQL load that skips files it already loaded. It suits thousands of files arriving in batches. Auto Loader (cloudFiles) is a streaming source that discovers new files incrementally, with schema inference and evolution. It suits continuous arrival and millions of files. Medallion: Bronze keeps raw data for replay, Silver holds cleaned and deduplicated data, Gold holds business aggregates. The point is recoverability: a Silver bug is fixed by reprocessing from Bronze, not by re-pulling the source. Unity Catalog: one governance layer for tables, files and models across workspaces, with grants, lineage and audit. Data modeling and warehousing 51. Implement SCD Type 2 with MERGE or in PySpark, and explain Types 1, 2 and 3. [Coforge, HDFC Bank, Deloitte, Ford, Wipro, Infosys, TCS, Capgemini, Databricks, Microsoft, Azure-role interviews] Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 keeps history with a new row per change, Type 3 adds a “previous value” column. Type 2 in one MERGE needs the staged-union trick: the change rows appear twice, once with the real key (to match and close the current row) and once with a null merge key (so they fall through to the insert branch): MERGE INTO dim_customer t USING ( SELECT s.customer_id AS merge_key, s.* FROM staged s UNION ALL SELECT NULL AS merge_key, s.* FROM staged s JOIN dim_customer d ON s.customer_id = d.customer_id WHERE d.is_current AND s.address <> d.address) u ON t.customer_id = u.merge_key AND t.is_current WHEN MATCHED AND t.address <> u.address THEN UPDATE SET is_current = false, end_date = u.effective_date WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, address, effective_date, end_date, is_current) VALUES (u.customer_id, u.address, u.effective_date, NULL, true); Follow-ups: compare a hash of tracked columns rather than each column, handle nulls in the comparison (use <=>), and decide what happens to late changes that arrive out of order. 52. Star vs snowflake schema, normalization vs denormalization, and many-to-many relationships in a star schema. [PwC, KPMG, Tiger Analytics, PayPal, HCLTech] A star schema has denormalised dimensions joined directly to the fact, which means fewer joins and simple BI queries. A snowflake normalises dimensions into sub-dimensions, which saves storage and keeps hierarchies consistent but costs joins. Lakehouse BI generally favours star. Many-to-many (an account with several holders) goes through a bridge table between fact and dimension, with a weighting factor if measures must not be double-counted. The data modeling guide covers grain and fact types. 53. Data lake vs warehouse vs mart vs lakehouse, and when to choose an RDBMS, NoSQL, a lake or a warehouse. [Wipro, TCS, PwC, Infosys, Grab, KPMG] A lake stores raw files of any shape cheaply. A warehouse stores modelled, governed tables for SQL. A mart is a subject-specific slice of the warehouse. A lakehouse puts table formats on lake storage to get warehouse guarantees (ACID, schema, time travel) without copying data into a separate system. Choose an RDBMS for transactional consistency and point lookups, NoSQL (DynamoDB, Cassandra) for key-value access at high write rates, and a lake or warehouse for scans and aggregation. 54. Design data models: retail sales by product, vendor, location and time; ride-sharing metrics; a real-time analytics model. [Amazon, Grab, Microsoft] Start with the grain: one row per order line, or per ride. The fact holds measures (quantity, revenue, duration), and dimensions are product, vendor, store, date and customer. Name additive versus non-additive measures. Ratios like average ride duration are computed, not stored. Then answer the follow-ups the interviewer will ask: which dimensions change (SCD), how to partition the fact (by date), and what changes at a billion rows (clustering on the common filter keys, pre-aggregated rollups). 55. Count distinct phone numbers over the last 90 or 180 days from a 100M-row table snapshotted daily, without scanning everything. [HDFC Bank] Do not scan 180 full snapshots. Build an incremental table of first-seen and last-seen dates per phone number, updated daily from the latest snapshot only. A 90-day count is then a filter on last_seen >= current_date - 90. If approximate is acceptable, keep a daily HyperLogLog sketch per day and merge 90 of them. Either way, the insight is to change the storage design so the query becomes cheap. Pipeline design and reliability 56. A pipeline fails halfway, or loads twice after a retry. How do you make it idempotent? [Coforge, EY, Amazon, Netflix, Atlassian, Ford] Running a step twice must give the same result as running it once: Overwrite by partition, not append: INSERT OVERWRITE the day you are loading, or Delta’s replaceWhere. MERGE on a business key for upserts. Commit atomically. Write to a staging location and swap, or rely on the table format’s commit, so a half-finished run leaves nothing visible. Track what was processed: a watermark or batch ID table updated in the same transaction as the data. For “the same financial transaction arrives twice” (Amazon), the key is a natural or producer-assigned transaction ID with a uniqueness check at write. 57. Incremental loading and CDC, including the case with no primary key and no timestamp. [PwC, Ford, Microsoft, Wipro, Infosys, EPAM, Cognizant, KPMG] With a reliable updated_at, store the high-water mark and pull rows above it, with a small overlap to catch clock skew. With log-based CDC (Debezium, ADF CDC, database change feeds), read the change stream with operation types and apply it with MERGE. With no key and no timestamp (EPAM), compute a hash of each full row, compare the current extract with the previous one, and treat new hashes as inserts and missing hashes as deletes.
