It costs a full extract each time, so say that the real fix is asking the source owner for a change column. 58. Late-arriving data in a table that has already been aggregated, or late cancellations in a Gold table. [Cognizant, Coforge, Walmart, Ford, PayPal, Tiger Analytics, Microsoft, Atlassian] Store data by event date, not load date. Each run re-aggregates every event date touched by newly arrived records, not just “yesterday”, and overwrites those Gold partitions. Keep a lookback window (for example, recompute the last 7 days every run) when late arrival is routine, and a targeted backfill for rare very late data. For dimensions that arrive after their facts, insert a placeholder dimension row and update it when the real one lands. 59. Handle schema drift and schema evolution without breaking downstream consumers. [Microsoft, Walmart, Ford, HCLTech, PwC, Netflix, Azure-role interviews] Separate tolerant ingestion from strict consumption. Bronze accepts new columns (schema evolution on write, or keep the raw payload in a string or VARIANT column). Silver and Gold have explicit contracts. Additive changes (a new nullable column) can flow through automatically. Breaking changes (rename, type narrowing, dropped column) should fail loudly at a validation step and alert, rather than silently produce nulls downstream. Mention a schema registry for streaming sources and data contracts with producers. 60. Data quality and reconciliation: source has 1 million rows, target has 990,000. Find out why. [Data QA interviews, Walmart, Wipro, Databricks, Deloitte, Ford] Reconcile stage by stage: counts and key sums at extract, Bronze, Silver and Gold. The stage where counts diverge locates the problem. Then check that stage’s filters, join types (an inner join to a dimension with missing keys is the classic loss), deduplication rules, rejected-record outputs and watermark logic. Identify the missing keys with an anti-join of source against target, and group them by an attribute to find the pattern. For ongoing checks: row-count, null-rate, uniqueness and freshness assertions that fail the pipeline, not just a dashboard. 61. A pipeline succeeds but the business metrics are wrong, or reports changed after a deployment. How do you debug it? [Netflix, Walmart, Wipro, Databricks] Treat it as a correctness incident. Pin down which metric, since when, and by how much. Diff the output of the previous code version and the new one on the same input. Most such bugs are join fan-out (duplicates multiplying a sum), a filter change, timezone handling at day boundaries, or a changed upstream definition. Then prevent recurrence with a regression test that compares key metrics on a fixed sample before deploy. 62. Data lineage and audit: track transformations across an eight-stage pipeline. [Wipro, Deloitte, Goldman Sachs, HCA Healthcare] Capture lineage automatically rather than documenting it: OpenLineage events from Spark and Airflow, or a catalog such as Unity Catalog that records table- and column-level lineage. Add run metadata (job ID, code version, input snapshot IDs) as columns or in an audit table, so any output row can be traced to the run and inputs that produced it. 63. Migrate an on-premise warehouse (Oracle, 500 TB, 10 years of history) to the cloud with minimal or zero downtime. [Deloitte, Walmart, Amazon] Bulk-copy history from a consistent snapshot, partitioned by date, and validate each partition with counts and checksums. Start CDC from the snapshot point so the target stays current. Run both systems in parallel and reconcile key reports daily. Cut consumers over in waves, starting with read-only analytics, and keep the old system as a rollback until sign-off. Mention transfer limits (500 TB over the network may need a physical transfer appliance), type mapping differences, and who signs off on reconciliation. 64. System design: process billions of payment transactions a day, with real-time fraud detection. [Paytm, Databricks, PayPal, Wipro] Shape the answer around the two consumers. Producers write to Kafka with an idempotent producer, keyed by account so per-account ordering holds. A streaming job scores transactions against features held in a low-latency store, and emits alerts. A separate path lands every event in a lakehouse table for reporting and model training, with MERGE on the transaction ID. Cover: partitioning by account, out-of-order events, exactly-once writes, replay from Kafka retention, PII handling, and reconciliation with the core banking ledger. 65. System design: one architecture for real-time order status and hourly analytics at 500 million orders a day. [Amazon, Coforge, Walmart, Ford, Grab, Comcast] Use a single event log (Kafka or Kinesis) with two consumers. A streaming job maintains current status per order in a key-value store for customer lookups. A second streaming or micro-batch job appends events to a lakehouse table partitioned by event hour, with hourly aggregates built on top. At about 6,000 orders per second on average, size for peak, not average. Discuss late events, idempotent upserts into the status store, and replaying from the log to rebuild either side. 66. Design a multi-tenant data platform, or a reusable ETL framework for 20 clients with different schemas. [Databricks, TCS, Deloitte] Make the pipeline metadata-driven: one engine, with per-client configuration for source, schema mapping, rules and schedule stored in tables, not code. Isolate tenants by catalog or schema with separate permissions, and tag compute for cost attribution. The trade-off to name: a shared framework cuts duplicated code but makes one client’s special case everyone’s risk. Version the framework, and allow plug-in transforms for exceptions. 67. Storage cost is exploding because the same purchase history is read 50 times a day by different jobs. [Amazon] The problem is repeated computation, not storage. Find the common transformation those 50 jobs perform, materialise it once as a curated table (or materialised view) partitioned and clustered for their access patterns, and point the jobs at it. Then tier cold history to cheaper storage classes. Back it with numbers: bytes scanned per day before and after. 68. What do you check before calling a pipeline production-ready, and how do you handle a 2 AM failure? [HCA Healthcare, Capgemini, Infosys, KPMG, PwC] Production-ready means: correct output validated against a source, idempotent reruns, alerts on failure and on lateness, data-quality checks, a documented backfill procedure, least-privilege access, and known cost per run. For the 2 AM failure: read the error and the failing step, check whether upstream data arrived, check recent changes, rerun safely if the cause was transient, and communicate the impact on downstream SLAs. Write up the root cause afterwards. Cloud services Azure 69. Azure IR vs self-hosted IR, integration runtime vs linked service, and Copy Activity vs Data Flows. [PwC, HDFC Bank, HCLTech] A linked service is connection information (where and how to connect). An integration runtime is the compute that runs the activity. The Azure IR is managed and reaches public or managed-private endpoints. A self-hosted IR is installed on your own machines to reach on-premise or private-network sources. An Azure-SSIS IR runs SSIS packages. Copy Activity moves data and is billed by data integration units and time. Mapping Data Flows run transformations on a managed Spark cluster, with cluster start-up time and per-core billing, so they cost more for simple copies. 70. An ADF pipeline is stuck in Queued, or fails every Monday at 6 AM but runs fine otherwise. Investigate. [PwC, Cognizant] Queued usually means it is waiting for capacity: pipeline or activity concurrency limits reached, a self-hosted IR node offline or saturated, or waiting on a dependency. Monday-only failures point at what is different on Mondays: a larger weekend backlog, a source system maintenance window, a credential or certificate rotated over the weekend, or another job scheduled at the same time competing for the same IR. Compare the Monday run’s inputs and timing with a good Tuesday run. 71. Secrets, masking and row-level security on Azure: Key Vault, dynamic data masking, Synapse RLS, and infrastructure as code. [PwC, HCLTech, Cognizant] Keep secrets in Key Vault and reference them from linked services and Databricks secret scopes, accessed with managed identities so no credential is in code. Dynamic data masking hides values at query time for unprivileged users. Row-level security uses a predicate function bound to a security policy to filter rows per user or client. Define all of it with Bicep or Terraform so environments are reproducible and reviewed. 72. Azure Databricks vs Synapse, and an end-to-end Blob → ADF → Databricks → Synapse → Power BI pipeline with its failure points. [EY, Cognizant] Databricks suits Spark engineering, streaming and ML on Delta. Synapse dedicated SQL pools suit a warehouse-first team with T-SQL skills. Many architectures use Databricks to transform and a SQL serving layer for BI. Failure points by stage: file arrival and partial files (Blob), IR capacity and credentials (ADF), cluster start-up, skew and schema changes (Databricks), load concurrency and statistics (Synapse), and refresh timeouts (Power BI). Each needs its own alert. GCP 73. BigQuery partitioning vs clustering, cost reduction, and MERGE. [Capgemini, HCA Healthcare, GCP-role interviews] Partitioning (by date, ingestion time or integer range) prunes whole partitions and makes cost predictable. Clustering sorts data within partitions by up to four columns, so filters on them read fewer blocks. Cost is driven by bytes scanned: select only needed columns, require partition filters, and use materialised views for repeated aggregates. MERGE in BigQuery follows standard SQL with WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses. 74. Airflow and Composer: operators, and what to do when upstream data has not arrived while the DAG is running. [HCA Healthcare, Capgemini, Walmart] Operators are the task types: they wrap an action (run a query, submit a Dataproc job, call an API) so a DAG is configuration, not custom code. For missing upstream data, use a sensor (in deferrable mode, so it does not hold a worker slot) with a timeout, alert when it times out, and keep downstream tasks from running on partial data. Rerunning must be idempotent. AWS 75. S3 storage classes, moving data between tiers, and DynamoDB vs RDS. [KPMG, AWS-role interviews] S3 offers Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and the Glacier classes (Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, Deep Archive). Lifecycle rules move objects by age automatically. Watch the minimum storage durations and retrieval charges on the infrequent and archive tiers. DynamoDB is a managed key-value store for predictable single-digit-millisecond access at any scale. RDS is a managed relational database for joins and transactions. Behavioural and managerial rounds These came up at nearly every company with a managerial round (PwC, KPMG, Deloitte, Cognizant, TCS, Infosys, Atlassian, Amazon, PayPal). The questions merge into eight: Walk through one end-to-end project: design, your decisions, challenges and impact. Tell me about a production failure you owned and what you changed afterwards. A technical decision you disagreed with. What evidence did you use? A time you took ownership beyond your role. How you handle conflicting requirements from stakeholders. Delivering under a tight deadline: what you cut, and the consequence. Explaining a technical problem (for example, data lag) to a non-technical client. A teammate’s mistake caused data loss. How do you handle it? Prepare two or three real stories and adapt them, rather than one answer per question. Use situation, action and result, and put a number in the result. Amazon’s bar raiser will test each story against its leadership principles, so expect “what data did you use” and “what would you do differently” follow-ups. Interview questions by component The sections above follow what the 29 companies asked. This section follows the component being tested instead, so you can drill one skill at a time: SQL, Python, Java, Scala, data modeling, system design, orchestration, warehouses and dbt, data quality, and LLM pipelines. These questions are not tied to a company. They come from the round types that recur in 2026 interview-preparation guides and public interview reviews (listed under References). They skip anything already answered above, and each one points back to the earlier question when the two overlap. Numbering continues from question 75. component round what the interviewer is really checking ───────────────── ───────────────────────────────────────────── SQL ──► correct results with ties, NULLs, duplicates Python ──► memory-safe processing, retries, clean code Java / Scala ──► JVM behaviour behind Spark, Kafka and Flink Data modeling ──► grain, history, keys that survive change System design ──► trade-offs, backfill, failure, cost over time Orchestration ──► idempotent, re-runnable scheduled work Warehouse and dbt ──► storage, incremental models, cost control Data quality ──► catching bad data before consumers do LLM pipelines ──► rate limits, retries and budgets as design inputs SQL 76. Sessionize a clickstream: start a new session when a user is idle for more than 30 minutes. Flag each event that starts a session, then number the sessions with a running sum of the flags: WITH flagged AS ( SELECT user_id, event_ts, CASE WHEN LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) IS NULL OR event_ts > LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) + INTERVAL '30' MINUTE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session FROM clicks ) SELECT user_id, event_ts, SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_no FROM flagged; The trap: the first event of each user has a NULL previous timestamp. If the IS NULL branch is missing, the comparison is unknown, the flag is 0, and the first session is numbered 0 instead of 1. The follow-up is late events. A late click can merge two sessions, so a streaming version needs a watermark and a session window, not this query. 77. Compute the median, and the 90th percentile, of order value per region. Standard SQL uses an ordered-set aggregate: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY order_value). PostgreSQL, Snowflake and Oracle support it. PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates between the two middle values, while PERCENTILE_DISC returns an actual value from the set. In Spark SQL, use percentile(order_value, 0.5) for an exact answer, percentile_approx(order_value, 0.9) for a bounded-memory approximation, or median(order_value), which was added in Spark 3.4. The trap: an exact percentile needs all of a group’s values in one place. On a skewed region that is a memory problem, which is why the approximate function exists. Say what accuracy the business needs before choosing. 78. Pivot monthly revenue into one column per month, then unpivot it back. Portable pivot with conditional aggregation: SELECT product_id, SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-01' THEN revenue END) AS jan, SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-02' THEN revenue END) AS feb, SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-03' THEN revenue END) AS mar FROM monthly_revenue GROUP BY product_id; Spark, Snowflake and SQL Server also have a PIVOT clause, and Spark and Snowflake have UNPIVOT. A portable unpivot is a UNION ALL of one SELECT per column, or a CROSS JOIN against a list of month labels. The trap: the pivot columns are fixed when the query is written. A new month needs new SQL, so a dynamic pivot belongs in the application or the BI tool. Note too that SUM with no ELSE returns NULL for a month with no sales, not 0. Say which one the report wants. 79. Build a monthly cohort retention table: of the users who signed up in each month, what share were active in each later month? WITH cohort AS ( SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(signup_ts)) AS cohort_month FROM users GROUP BY user_id ), activity AS ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', event_ts) AS active_month FROM events ) SELECT c.cohort_month, DATEDIFF(month, c.cohort_month, a.active_month) AS month_offset, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) * 1.0 / MAX(COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)) OVER (PARTITION BY c.cohort_month) AS retention FROM cohort c JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = c.user_id AND a.active_month >= c.cohort_month GROUP BY c.cohort_month, DATEDIFF(month, c.cohort_month, a.active_month); The denominator is the cohort’s size, which here is the offset-0 count. The month-difference function is dialect-specific: DATEDIFF(month, a, b) in Snowflake and SQL Server, months_between in Spark, AGE arithmetic in PostgreSQL. The trap: using offset 0 as the cohort size assumes every user is active in their signup month. If that is not guaranteed, compute the cohort size from cohort directly and join it in. 80. Month-over-month revenue growth as a percentage, without dividing by zero. SELECT month, revenue, LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue, 100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0) AS mom_pct FROM monthly_revenue; NULLIF(x, 0) turns a zero denominator into NULL, so the result is NULL rather than an error. The first month has no previous row, so its growth is also NULL. The trap: a missing month. LAG takes the previous row, not the previous calendar month. If March has no row, April is compared with February. Join to a calendar or date dimension first so every month exists. 81. A report's totals doubled after someone added a join. Why, and how do you find it? The join fanned out. Joining orders to a table with more than one row per order key (several shipments, several payment attempts, a Type 2 dimension joined on the business key alone) repeats each order once per match, and SUM(order_amount) counts it several times. To find it, check the key’s uniqueness on the joined side: SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM shipments GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Then compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) after the join. Fixes, in order of preference: aggregate the many side to the order grain before joining, join to exactly one row (the latest shipment with ROW_NUMBER), or for a Type 2 dimension add the validity-interval condition. The related trap: a filter on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN placed in WHERE removes the unmatched rows and silently turns it into an inner join. Put that condition in the ON clause. Python 82. Generators: what does yield do, and why does it matter for data pipelines? A function containing yield returns a generator. Calling it runs nothing. Each next() resumes the function until the next yield, so values are produced one at a time and the function’s local state is kept between calls. def read_records(path): with open(path) as fh: for line in fh: yield parse(line) def valid(records): return (r for r in records if r["amount"] is not None) for batch in chunked(valid(read_records("orders.jsonl")), 10_000): write(batch) Memory stays proportional to one batch, not to the file. This is the answer to “process a 20 GB file on a 4 GB machine” (question 17). The trap: a generator can be consumed only once. Calling len() on it, or iterating it twice, gives a TypeError or an empty second pass. 83. What is wrong with def add_tag(tag, tags=[])? The default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, not on each call. Every call that omits tags shares the same list, so tags from earlier calls leak into later ones: def add_tag(tag, tags=[]): tags.append(tag) return tags add_tag("a") # ['a'] add_tag("b") # ['a', 'b'] Use None as the default and create the list inside the function. The same bug appears with a dict default used as a cache, which is sometimes deliberate and should then be commented as such. 84. Shallow copy vs deep copy, and is vs ==. copy.copy(x) creates a new outer object but shares the nested objects, so changing a nested list through the copy changes the original. copy.deepcopy(x) copies recursively. list(x), x[:] and dict(x) are all shallow. == compares values by calling __eq__. is compares identity, whether two names point at the same object. Use is only for singletons such as None. a == b can be true while a is b is false. The trap: small integers and some strings are cached by CPython, so a is b can appear to work in a test and then fail on other values. Never use is for numbers or strings. 85. Write an idempotent extractor for a paginated REST API with rate limits. The shape interviewers expect: import random, time, requests def fetch_all(url, params, max_retries=6): cursor = load_checkpoint() # resume where the last run stopped while True: for attempt in range(max_retries): resp = requests.get(url, params={**params, "cursor": cursor}, timeout=30) if resp.status_code == 429 or resp.status_code >= 500: wait = float(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt)) time.sleep(wait + random.uniform(0, 1)) # backoff with jitter continue resp.raise_for_status() # other 4xx: fail loudly break else: raise RuntimeError("retries exhausted") page = resp.json() write_page(page["items"]) # upsert on a natural key, not append cursor = page.get("next_cursor") save_checkpoint(cursor) # only after the page is stored if not cursor: return What makes it idempotent: records are upserted on a key, and the checkpoint moves only after a page is written, so a crash re-fetches at most one page and re-applying it changes nothing. The traps: retrying on every 4xx (a 401 will never succeed), backing off without jitter (all workers retry at the same instant), and offset-based pagination over data that changes during the run, which skips or repeats rows. Prefer cursor-based pagination when the API offers it. 86. A plain Python UDF makes a PySpark job ten times slower. Why, and what are the alternatives? A Python UDF runs in a separate Python worker process next to each executor. Rows are serialized from the JVM to Python and the results back again, one row at a time, and Catalyst cannot see inside the function to optimize or push filters through it. The options, best first: Built-in functions (F.when, F.regexp_extract, F.transform) stay in the JVM and are optimized. A pandas UDF (@pandas_udf) moves data in Arrow batches and runs vectorized pandas code, which removes most of the per-row cost. A Scala or Java UDF registered in the JVM avoids the Python boundary entirely. The trap: a pandas UDF still crosses a process boundary. When a built-in function exists, it beats any UDF. 87. Validate incoming records in Python before loading them. Declare the schema once and validate at the boundary. A dataclass with type hints documents the shape but does not check it at runtime. A validation library such as Pydantic does: from datetime import datetime from decimal import Decimal from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError class Order(BaseModel): order_id: str amount: Decimal ordered_at: datetime good, bad = [], [] for raw in records: try: good.append(Order(**raw)) except ValidationError as e: bad.append({"raw": raw, "error": str(e)}) # quarantine, do not drop Bad records go to a quarantine table with the error, so the load continues and someone can fix and replay them. Alert when the quarantine rate crosses a threshold. Silently dropping rows is what produces question 60’s missing 10,000. Java Java comes up in rounds for teams that run Spark, Kafka, Flink or Hadoop on the JVM, and in banks such as American Express that run a separate fundamentals round. 88. How does HashMap work internally, and what changed in Java 8? A HashMap is an array of buckets. put(k, v) computes k.hashCode(), mixes the high bits into the low bits, and uses hash & (capacity - 1) as the bucket index. Capacity is always a power of two. Entries that land in the same bucket form a linked list, and equals() finds the right one. When the number of entries passes capacity * loadFactor (default load factor 0.75, default capacity 16), the table doubles and entries are redistributed. Since Java 8, a bucket whose list grows past 8 entries is converted to a red-black tree, provided the table has at least 64 buckets. That turns the worst case for a heavily colliding bucket from O(n) to O(log n). The follow-up: HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent writes can lose entries or corrupt the structure. Use ConcurrentHashMap (next question). 89. HashMap vs Hashtable vs Collections.synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap. HashMap: not synchronized; allows one null key and null values. Hashtable: a legacy class; every method is synchronized on the whole table; no null keys or values. Collections.synchronizedMap(map): a wrapper that locks one mutex around every call. Iteration still needs a manual synchronized block. ConcurrentHashMap: since Java 8, it uses CAS to insert into an empty bucket and locks only the first node of a bucket otherwise, so writers to different buckets do not block each other. Reads do not lock. Iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException. No null keys or values. The trap: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is a race even on a ConcurrentHashMap, because two threads can both pass the check. Use the atomic putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent or merge. 90. JVM memory areas and garbage collection, and how they show up in a Spark executor. Heap: objects. It is split into a young generation (new objects, collected often) and an old generation (long-lived objects). Metaspace: class metadata, in native memory since Java 8, replacing PermGen. Thread stacks: one per thread, holding frames and local variables. Deep recursion gives StackOverflowError. Direct and native memory: off-heap buffers used by Netty, Arrow and Spark’s off-heap mode. G1 has been the default collector since Java 9. It splits the heap into regions and collects the ones with the most garbage first, against a pause target. In Spark, a long GC pause shows up as high “GC Time” for a task in the UI, and in the worst case as an executor lost after missed heartbeats. A container killed by YARN or Kubernetes for exceeding its memory limit is usually off-heap growth, which is what spark.executor.memoryOverhead covers. More heap does not fix it. See question 33. 91. The equals() and hashCode() contract, and what happens when a key is mutated. If a.equals(b) is true, a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). The reverse is not required. Overriding equals without hashCode breaks every hash-based collection: two equal keys land in different buckets, so get misses and a HashSet holds duplicates. If a field used in hashCode changes after the object is inserted into a HashMap, the entry stays in the old bucket. get with the same object then looks in the new bucket and returns null, and the entry leaks. Make keys immutable. Java record types and Scala case classes generate a consistent equals and hashCode from immutable fields. 92. volatile vs synchronized vs AtomicLong. volatile guarantees visibility: a write by one thread is seen by later reads in other threads, and it is not reordered. It does not make count++ atomic, because that is a read, an add and a write. synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility for a block. It is correct, and it serializes the threads. AtomicLong and the other atomics use compare-and-swap to make single-variable updates such as incrementAndGet() atomic without a lock. Under heavy contention, LongAdder spreads updates across cells and is faster for counters. The classic use of volatile is a stop flag read by a worker loop. The classic bug is a volatile int counter that loses increments. 93. Why does Spark throw "Task not serializable", and how do you fix it? org.apache.spark.SparkException: Task not serializable means a closure sent to the executors refers to an object that does not implement Serializable. The most common case: a lambda inside a class uses a field or method of that class, so the whole enclosing instance is captured, together with its non-serializable members (a database connection, a logger, the SparkContext). Fixes: Copy the needed field into a local variable before the lambda, so only that value is captured. Mark members that should not travel as transient, and create them lazily on the executor. Create per-partition resources, such as a connection, inside mapPartitions or foreachPartition, not on the driver. Make small helper classes Serializable, or use static methods or a Scala object. The stack trace’s “Serialization stack” lists the exact chain of fields that pulled the object in. Read it from the bottom. 94. Java Streams: lazy evaluation, and when parallelStream() is a bad idea. Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) build a pipeline and run nothing. A terminal operation (collect, count, forEach) pulls elements through it, fused into one pass. This is the same idea as Spark’s transformations and actions (question 21), inside one JVM. parallelStream() splits the work across the common ForkJoinPool. It hurts when the source splits badly (a LinkedList, or I/O), when the per-element work is tiny, when the lambda has side effects on shared state, or inside a server where every request shares the same pool. Inside a Spark task it competes with Spark’s own task threads for the executor’s cores. Scala 95. What does a case class give you, and why does Spark use them? A case class generates equals, hashCode and toString from its constructor fields, a companion apply (no new needed), copy with named arguments, and unapply for pattern matching. Its fields are vals, so instances are immutable by default. Spark derives an Encoder for a case class, so ds.as[Order] gives a typed Dataset[Order] with compile-time field checks, while the data stays in Spark’s binary row format. The trap: a typed lambda such as ds.filter(_.amount > 100) is opaque to Catalyst, so the filter is not pushed to the Parquet reader. The column expression ds.filter($"amount" > 100) is pushed down. Use typed lambdas where type safety matters more than pushdown. 96. val vs var vs lazy val vs def. val: evaluated once, at definition, and cannot be reassigned. var: mutable. Avoid it in shared or Spark code. lazy val: evaluated once, on first access, and then cached. Thread-safe initialization has a small locking cost. def: re-evaluated on every call. A lazy val inside a Scala object is a common way to create one expensive resource per executor JVM, such as a client or a connection pool, without serializing it from the driver (see question 93). 97. Option vs null, and map vs flatMap vs a for-comprehension. Option[T] is Some(value) or None, so absence is part of the type and the compiler makes the caller handle it. Option(x) turns a Java null into None. map transforms the value inside. flatMap is for functions that themselves return an Option, so you get Option[B] instead of Option[Option[B]]. A for-comprehension is syntax for a chain of flatMap calls and a final map: for { user <- findUser(id) // Option[User] email <- user.email // Option[String] } yield email.toLowerCase // Option[String] The trap: opt.get on None throws NoSuchElementException. Use getOrElse, fold or pattern matching. 98. Implicits in Scala 2 and given/using in Scala 3: what are they, and where does Spark rely on them? An implicit parameter is filled in by the compiler from values marked implicit in scope. An implicit conversion or an implicit class adds methods to an existing type. Scala 3 splits these uses apart: given instances and using parameters for context, and extension methods for added syntax. Spark depends on implicits through import spark.implicits._. That import provides the Encoder instances behind toDF(), toDS() and as[T], and the $"col" string interpolator. The version detail: Spark 3.5 is built for Scala 2.12 and 2.13, and Spark 4 for Scala 2.13 only. Spark does not publish Scala 3 builds, so Spark code still uses Scala 2 implicits. The forgotten-import error is Unable to find encoder for type. 99. Trait vs abstract class. A class can mix in several traits but extend only one class. Traits are how Scala composes behaviour: logging, retry, metrics. In Scala 2, a trait cannot take constructor parameters; Scala 3 allows them. An abstract class can take constructor parameters and is easier to call from Java. Use a trait for a capability that mixes into many types. Use an abstract class for a base type that needs constructor arguments, or Java interop. Mention linearization when several traits override the same method: the rightmost trait in the mix-in order wins, and super calls go right to left. 100. Write a tail-recursive function, and say what @tailrec guarantees. import scala.annotation.tailrec def sum(xs: List[Long]): Long = { @tailrec def loop(rest: List[Long], acc: Long): Long = rest match { case Nil => acc case h :: t => loop(t, acc + h) // the recursive call is the last action } loop(xs, 0L) } A call in tail position is compiled into a loop, so the stack does not grow. @tailrec does not create the optimization. It makes the compiler fail if the call is not in tail position, so a later edit cannot silently bring back a StackOverflowError. In practice, foldLeft does the same job in one line. Data modeling These build on questions 51 to 54. The data modeling guide covers each topic in depth with runnable examples. 101. Model a sales fact for five sales channels and three product hierarchies. What is the grain? Declare the grain first: one row per order line, the lowest level the source records. Channel becomes a dim_channel foreign key, not five separate fact tables, so cross-channel totals are a plain GROUP BY. Product hierarchies (category, brand, merchandising group) are attributes of dim_product, or separate hierarchy tables if they are ragged or change independently. The fact holds only the product key. A hierarchy is a property of the product, not of the sale. If one channel records data at a coarser level (wholesale reports daily totals, not lines), do not mix that into the line-level fact. Build a second fact at the daily grain, and conform the shared dimensions so the two can be compared. 102. Role-playing, junk and degenerate dimensions. Role-playing dimension: one physical dimension used in several roles. An order fact has order_date_key, ship_date_key and delivery_date_key, all pointing at dim_date, usually exposed as three views named for the role. Junk dimension: a small dimension that combines low-cardinality flags and indicators (is_gift, payment_type, promo_flag) into one row per combination, so the fact holds one key instead of many flag columns. Degenerate dimension: a dimension key with no dimension table, such as order_number stored on the fact. It is used for grouping lines into an order and for tracing back to the source. 103. What are conformed dimensions, and what is a bus matrix? A conformed dimension has the same keys, attribute names and meanings in every fact that uses it. dim_customer in sales and in support tickets then gives results that can be compared, and “drilling across” both facts by customer segment is valid. The bus matrix is the planning grid: business processes as rows (orders, shipments, returns), shared dimensions as columns (date, customer, product), and a mark where a process uses a dimension. It shows which dimensions must be conformed before teams build facts separately. Without one, each team builds its own customer dimension and the numbers stop agreeing. 104. SCD Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 6: how do you choose? Ask how the business reports history: Type 1 when only the current value matters, or the change is a correction. History is restated. Type 2 when facts must report under the value valid at the time, for example sales by the region the customer was in when they bought. Type 6 when users need both “as was” and “as is” on the same row: Type 2 version rows, plus a current-value column overwritten on every version, so no extra join is needed for current reporting. The choice is per attribute, not per table. email can be Type 1 while loyalty_tier is Type 2 in the same dimension. Question 51 covers the MERGE implementation. 105. A fact arrives before its dimension row (an early-arriving fact). What do you load? Never drop the fact and never load a NULL key. Two standard options: Unknown member. Point the fact at a reserved key such as -1 (“Unknown”). Reprocess the fact when the dimension arrives. Inferred member. Insert a placeholder dimension row with the business key and default attributes, flagged is_inferred = true. When the real row arrives, overwrite the placeholder in place (a Type 1 update, even for a Type 2 dimension), so the fact’s key stays valid. The inferred member avoids reprocessing facts, and is the more common answer. Monitor the count of inferred rows that never get completed. 106. One big table (OBT) vs a star schema in a lakehouse. An OBT pre-joins the fact with its dimension attributes into one wide table. Columnar formats read only the columns a query needs, and compression handles the repeated values well, so wide tables are cheaper than they were in a row store. Dashboards get simple, join-free SQL. What an OBT costs: a Type 1 dimension change means rewriting every fact row that carries the attribute; history semantics are fixed when the table is built; and every new attribute is a backfill. A defensible answer keeps the star as the source of truth and derives OBTs for specific dashboards. The OBT can then be rebuilt from the star at any time. System design Expect one system design round at most product companies. The 2026 guides describe it as the round that carries the most weight. The follow-ups are predictable: why this storage layer, what you ruled out, how backfill works, what breaks when a source changes, and what it costs over time. 107. Design a pipeline that ingests 1 TB of clickstream a day and serves dashboards at under 2 seconds P95. Start with the numbers. 1 TB a day is about 12 MB/s on average, so plan for 3 to 5 times that at peak. Then go layer by layer: SDK / web ──► Kafka (partition by user_id) ──► stream job ──► bronze table │ (append, raw) ▼ silver: deduplicated, sessionized events │ ▼ gold: pre-aggregated by minute/hour × dimension ──► serving store (OLAP engine) The key decision is that the dashboards do not scan raw events. Two seconds at P95 comes from pre-aggregated gold tables, or from a real-time OLAP store such as Druid, Pinot or ClickHouse, not from a lake query over a terabyte. Cover deduplication by event ID, late events with a watermark, a schema registry for the event contract, partitioning by event date, and compaction of the small files from streaming writes (question 36). The follow-ups: how many Kafka partitions (from peak throughput per partition and consumer parallelism), and how you replay a day after a bug (re-read bronze, not Kafka, once retention has passed). 108. Backfill nine months of history after a logic fix, without double counting and without stopping the daily job. Make every run partition-scoped and overwrite-based. Each run replaces one date partition (INSERT OVERWRITE, Delta replaceWhere, Iceberg dynamic overwrite). A backfill is then many runs of the normal job with old dates, and reruns are safe. Write to a shadow table or branch first. Backfill into a copy (or an Iceberg branch), reconcile row counts and totals against the old output, then swap atomically. Throttle it. Run in date batches with limited concurrency, so the backfill does not starve the daily SLA. Run the newest months first if consumers care most about them. Freeze the inputs. Read from a snapshot or bronze, not from a source that is still changing. The trap: appending recomputed data on top of the old output. That is the double count. 109. An upstream API changes a field from a string to an object, and the pipeline starts failing. What do you do in the next hour? In order: Stop the damage. Pause the job, or let it fail closed. Do not let it write partial or mis-parsed data into tables consumers read. Keep the raw data. Make sure bronze is still landing the raw payloads, so nothing is lost while you fix the parser. Tell people. Post to the consumer channel: which tables are stale, since when, and the next update time. Fix forward. Parse both shapes, mapping the old string to the new object’s field, and route anything unparseable to quarantine. Replay from bronze for the affected window, then verify counts. Afterwards: a schema contract with the producer, a schema check at ingestion that alerts before the transform fails, and a test with the new payload. Question 59 covers schema evolution in general. 110. Design CDC replication from a PostgreSQL OLTP database into a lakehouse table. PostgreSQL WAL ──► Debezium (logical replication slot) ──► Kafka topic per table │ initial snapshot ─────────────────────────────────────┤ ▼ Spark / Flink: order by LSN per key, MERGE into table Points to cover: Initial snapshot plus stream. Take a consistent snapshot, then apply changes from the log position where the snapshot ended. Ordering. Apply changes per primary key in log order (LSN), and keep the latest LSN on the target row, so a replayed or late event older than the stored one is ignored. Deletes. Apply them as deletes or soft-delete flags. Handle the tombstone records Kafka uses for compaction. Operational risk. A replication slot that nobody consumes keeps WAL on the primary until the disk fills. Monitor slot lag. The data modeling guide runs an idempotent CDC apply end to end. 111. Estimate storage and cost at one, three and ten years for a 500 GB-a-day source. Interviewers want arithmetic, stated assumptions and the levers that change it: Raw: 500 GB a day × 365 ≈ 180 TB a year. As compressed Parquet at an assumed 5:1 ratio: about 36 TB a year, so about 110 TB at three years and 360 TB at ten, before copies. Multiply by the layers you keep (bronze, silver, gold) and by time travel or snapshot retention, which keeps old files alive. Then the levers: lifecycle rules that move old bronze to colder storage classes, a retention policy per layer, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup, and aggregating old detail when nobody queries it. Compute usually costs more than storage, so mention the incremental processing that avoids recomputing history every day. State the compression ratio as an assumption to be measured on a sample. Real ratios depend on the data. 112. Design an event deduplication layer for at-least-once delivery at billions of events a day. At-least-once delivery means duplicates are normal, so deduplication is a design component, not a cleanup job. Key. Use a producer-assigned event ID. Without one, hash the business fields, and accept that identical genuine events will merge. Window. In streaming, keep the seen IDs in state with a TTL or watermark (dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark in Spark 3.5), sized to the longest realistic redelivery delay. Sink. Make the write idempotent too: MERGE on the event ID, or a primary key in the serving store, which catches duplicates that arrive after the state has expired. Measure. Track the duplicate rate. A sudden rise usually means a producer retry storm, not more traffic. Questions 38 and 39 cover exactly-once for payments and Kafka. Orchestration and Airflow 113. How do you make an Airflow DAG idempotent? Each task run must process a fixed, well-defined slice of data and produce the same output however many times it runs. Use the data interval, not the clock. Read data_interval_start and data_interval_end from the context (or `` in templates) instead of calling datetime.now(). A rerun of last Tuesday then processes last Tuesday. Overwrite the slice the task owns (a date partition), or MERGE on a key. Never append. Keep tasks atomic. Write to staging and swap, so a failed task leaves nothing half-written for the retry to trip over. The trap: a task that “loads everything since the last run” using a watermark stored outside Airflow. A manual rerun of an old interval then loads the wrong data. 114. catchup, backfill, and what happens when you deploy a DAG with a start_date in the past. With catchup=True, the scheduler creates a run for every interval between start_date and now that has not run yet. Deploying a daily DAG with a start_date a year ago creates 365 runs at once. With catchup=False, only the latest interval runs. Set it explicitly on every DAG: the default comes from catchup_by_default, which Airflow 3 changed from True to False, so the same DAG behaves differently after an upgrade. Control it with max_active_runs, pools and task concurrency, and run deliberate backfills with the backfill command, so history is reprocessed in a throttled way. Airflow 3 runs backfills through the scheduler, where earlier versions ran them in a separate CLI process. The trap: catchup on a DAG that is not idempotent (question 113). Every catch-up run then loads the same “latest” data. 115. Sensors: poke vs reschedule vs deferrable, and why sensors can deadlock a cluster. Poke mode holds a worker slot for the sensor’s whole wait, checking on an interval. Reschedule mode releases the slot between checks and is rescheduled for the next one. Deferrable operators hand the wait to the triggerer process, which watches many waits asynchronously, and use no worker slot at all until the condition fires. If many poke-mode sensors wait on files that arrive late, they can occupy every worker slot, and the tasks that would produce those files cannot start. Use deferrable sensors for long waits, set a timeout, and decide what a timeout means: fail and alert, or skip. Question 74 covers the “upstream data has not arrived” scenario. 116. What is XCom for, and what should you never put in it? XCom passes small values between tasks: a file path, a row count, a batch ID. Values are stored in the metadata database by default. Do not pass datasets through XCom. Large values bloat the metadata database and slow the scheduler and UI. Write the data to object storage or a table and pass its location. If you need large XComs, a custom XCom backend can store the payload in object storage and keep only a reference in the database. 117. What changed in Airflow 3, and what does an interviewer expect you to know about it? Airflow 3.0 was released in April 2025. The changes that come up: Assets replace Datasets as the name for data-aware scheduling: a DAG can run when an upstream asset is updated, not only on a timetable. DAG versioning: the UI shows which version of a DAG’s code each run used. Task SDK and execution API: tasks talk to the scheduler through an API instead of connecting to the metadata database directly, which is what makes remote and multi-language execution possible. Removals: SubDAGs, SLA callbacks and the execution_date context key are gone. Use TaskGroups, deadline alerts or external monitoring, and dag_run.logical_date. Also mention dynamic task mapping (.expand(), from Airflow 2.3): it creates one task instance per input at runtime, for example one per file. Warehouses: Snowflake and dbt 118. What is a Snowflake micro-partition, and how does clustering affect query performance? Snowflake stores each table as micro-partitions: immutable, columnar units of 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, created automatically in load order. For every micro-partition it keeps metadata, including each column’s min and max values. A query with a filter skips the micro-partitions whose range cannot match. That is pruning, and it is the main performance lever. Pruning works only if the data is laid out so that ranges do not overlap much. Data loaded in date order prunes well on date and badly on customer_id. A clustering key (ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (col)) has Automatic Clustering rewrite micro-partitions in the background to reduce overlap. It costs credits, so use it only on large tables with a dominant filter. Check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION before and after. 119. Permanent vs transient vs temporary tables in Snowflake. Permanent: Time Travel (1 day by default, up to 90 on Enterprise edition) plus a 7-day Fail-safe period. Transient: persists until dropped, Time Travel of 0 or 1 day, and no Fail-safe. Temporary: exists only for the session, Time Travel of 0 or 1 day, no Fail-safe. Use transient tables for staging and intermediate data that can be rebuilt. Fail-safe storage is billed, so a frequently rewritten permanent staging table pays for seven days of old versions nobody will restore. 120. Snowflake streams vs tasks. A stream is change tracking on a table: it records the inserts, updates and deletes since its offset, exposed with METADATA$ACTION and METADATA$ISUPDATE columns. Consuming the stream in a DML statement advances the offset when the transaction commits. A task is scheduled SQL: a cron schedule or interval, optionally chained into a graph of tasks, and optionally conditioned on SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('stream_name'), so it runs only when there are changes. Together they give incremental ELT inside Snowflake: the stream says what changed, and the task merges it into the target on a schedule. 121. A Snowflake virtual warehouse is expensive. How do you tell whether it is the right size? Look at the query history and profiles before changing the size: Spilling to local or remote storage in the query profile means the warehouse is too small for those queries. Scale up. Queuing (queued time in query history) with short queries means too much concurrency. Scale out with a multi-cluster warehouse, rather than up. Low utilization, with a warehouse running between sparse queries, means auto-suspend is too long. Lower it, because billing is per second with a 60-second minimum each time it resumes. Poor pruning (partitions scanned close to partitions total) means the query or the layout is the problem, and no size fixes it. Separate workloads (ELT, BI, ad hoc) onto separate warehouses, so each can be sized and attributed, and set resource monitors as a spend backstop. 122. dbt incremental models: how do they work, and what goes wrong? An incremental model builds the full table on the first run. On later runs is_incremental() is true, and the model selects only new or changed rows: {{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id', incremental_strategy='merge') }} SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }} {% if is_incremental() %} WHERE updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM {{ this }}) {% endif %} With a unique_key and the merge strategy, changed rows update in place instead of duplicating. The strategies available (append, merge, delete+insert, insert_overwrite) depend on the adapter. What goes wrong: late-arriving rows with an updated_at older than the current max are skipped forever, so subtract a lookback window. A model logic change does not fix history until you run with --full-refresh. And without a unique_key, every rerun appends duplicates. 123. dbt snapshots and dbt tests. A snapshot implements SCD Type 2 on a source table. Each run compares the current rows with the stored versions, using the timestamp strategy (an updated_at column) or the check strategy (a list of columns), and closes changed versions with dbt_valid_to while inserting new ones with dbt_valid_from. Snapshots only see the state at run time, so changes between two runs are lost. CDC catches every change; a snapshot catches only the state at each run. Tests are assertions run as queries. The generic ones are unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships (referential integrity). Singular tests are SQL files that should return zero rows. Put unique and not_null on every model’s grain key, which is the cheapest protection against the fan-out in question 81. Model contracts can also enforce column names and types at build time. Data quality and observability 124. What do you monitor on a production table, and where do the alerts go? Five signals cover most incidents: Freshness: the last successful load time against the SLA. Volume: the row count against its usual range for that day of the week. Schema: added, removed or retyped columns. Distribution: null rate, distinct counts and value ranges on key columns. Lineage: which upstream tables feed it, so a failure can be traced to its source and its downstream impact listed. Alerts go to the team that owns the table, with the table name, the failed check, the expected and actual values, and a runbook link. Route by severity: a page only for broken SLAs on critical tables, a channel message for the rest. An alert nobody acts on should be deleted or fixed, because alert fatigue hides the real one. 125. What is the write-audit-publish (WAP) pattern? Write new data somewhere consumers cannot see it, audit it with quality checks, and publish it atomically only if the checks pass. In Iceberg, write to a branch (or stage a snapshot with spark.wap.id), run the checks against the branch, then fast-forward main to it. In Delta, or in any table format, write to a staging table and swap or MERGE after the checks pass. dbt’s equivalent is building into a separate schema and swapping it in. Failed data never reaches a dashboard, and the failed batch stays available for debugging. The cost is extra latency and the storage for the staged data. 126. A producer team wants to rename a column you consume. How does a data contract handle it? A data contract is an agreed, versioned specification of a dataset: the schema, the meaning of each field, the quality guarantees, the SLA and the owner. It is enforced in CI for the producer, so a breaking change fails their build before it reaches you. A rename is a breaking change. The contract process is to add the new column, keep publishing the old one (deprecated) for an agreed period, tell consumers, and then remove the old column in a new major version. Question 59 covers the consumer side. LLM and AI data pipelines These are newer. They appear in 2026 interview guides for teams that feed models or run LLM calls inside pipelines. 127. Design a pipeline that processes 10,000 documents a day through an LLM, within rate limits, retries and a cost budget. Treat the LLM as a slow, rate-limited, metered external API: Queue the work. Put document IDs on a queue, and have a pool of workers sized to the provider’s request and token limits, not to the document count. Back off on 429 and 5xx, with jitter and a retry cap (question 85). Send documents that keep failing to a dead-letter queue. Make it idempotent and cached. Key results by document ID plus content hash plus prompt version, so a retry or rerun does not pay twice, and only changed documents are reprocessed. Budget explicitly. Estimate tokens per document, track spend per run, and stop or degrade (a smaller model, a summary first) when the daily budget is reached. Validate the output. Parse it against a schema and quarantine invalid responses, as in question 87. Store the prompt version and model ID with each result, so outputs can be traced and regenerated when either changes. 128. Keep a vector index in sync with a source table of documents. This is CDC again, with an embedding step: Detect changes with a change feed or a content hash per document, and re-embed only new or changed documents. Chunk deterministically, with chunk IDs derived from the document ID and position, so a re-embed replaces the old chunks instead of adding to them. Propagate deletes. A document deleted at the source must be deleted from the index, or retrieval keeps returning it. This is the case most often forgotten. Version the embedding model. A new model needs a full re-embed into a new index, then a cutover, because vectors from two models cannot be compared. How to prepare from this list Start with the frequency table. Window functions, skew, idempotency, late data and incremental loads appear at most companies. Being solid on those five covers most rounds. Prepare by company type. For product companies, practise designing systems out loud and coding without an IDE. For services and consulting firms, know Azure Data Factory and Databricks operationally, implement SCD Type 2 from memory, and prepare the managerial stories. Answer scenarios with evidence. For every “it became slow” or “the numbers are wrong” question, the structure is the same: what changed, where you look, what you found, what you fixed, and how you verified it. That structure is what these interviews reward. Then drill by component. Once the company-tagged questions are solid, use the component section to cover the rounds your target companies run: Java or Scala for JVM-heavy teams, Snowflake and dbt for analytics-engineering roles, and system design for every senior role. Do not memorise answers. Interviewers change one condition (“now the key is null”, “now there is no timestamp”) and watch whether the answer adapts. Every outline above names the mechanism so you can reason from it. References Spark SQL performance tuning for AQE, join strategies and partition settings Spark configuration for memory and shuffle defaults Structured Streaming programming guide for watermarks, checkpoints and output semantics Delta Lake documentation for the transaction log, MERGE, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM Data engineering interview questions and answers for 2026 (Dataquest) for the round types and question styles used in the component section Data engineer interview questions 2026 (KORE1) for the system design follow-ups, Snowflake and backfill scenarios Data engineering interview prep 2026 (DEV Community) for the LLM-pipeline design prompt Snowflake micro-partitions and data clustering and Snowflake storage costs for Time Travel and Fail-safe dbt incremental models and dbt snapshots Apache Airflow 3 release notes for assets, DAG versioning and the removed features Java HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap API documentation Top Apache Spark interview questions for 200 Spark questions answered in depth Data modeling for data engineers for grain, SCD and fact types Trademarks Apache Spark, Apache Kafka, Apache Hudi, Apache Iceberg, Apache Airflow, Apache Parquet, Apache ORC, Apache Avro and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries.
