Begin with the business process and declare what one row means before choosing columns, keys, or partitions. Keep measurements at a consistent grain. Put descriptive, filterable attributes in dimensions and store facts that can be aggregated correctly. Use stable business keys to identify source entities and surrogate keys to identify warehouse dimension versions. They solve different problems. For Type 2 history, join each fact to the dimension version valid at the event time. An equality join on customer ID alone silently rewrites history. CDC is a capture mechanism, not a target model. Snapshots establish a base; ordered log changes maintain state and history. A logical model is separate from indexes, partitions, shards, file ordering, and lakehouse table formats. Choose each physical technique from measured query and operational requirements. Data mesh and data fabric address different architectural concerns, while lineage and metadata make ownership, dependencies, and impact discoverable. Every part ends with interview questions and model answers, and a final round of design scenarios ties the parts together. How to use this guide A dashboard that reports twice the real revenue rarely has a Spark bug behind it. The usual cause is a model that never said what one row means. This guide builds that discipline from the first definition up to lakehouse layout, using one running example: an online shop’s order lines, customers, and products. Each section is layered so you can stop at the depth you need: In plain terms opens a section with the idea in one or two sentences and an everyday example. The mechanism follows: what the engine or the pipeline actually does, and what the choice costs. Run it gives a complete script or SQL file, with the output it produced when this guide was verified. Interview questions close every part, as collapsible questions with the answer an interviewer is listening for. Beginner: Part 1, then sections 2.1 to 2.3. You should be able to explain grain, keys, cardinality, normal forms, facts and dimensions, and star versus snowflake. Intermediate: sections 2.2.1 to 2.4, then 3.1 to 3.3. You should be able to choose a fact shape, classify measures, build SCD Type 2 with MERGE, apply CDC idempotently, and explain the medallion layers. Advanced: section 3.4 to the end. You should be able to defend contracts and schema evolution, Lambda versus Kappa, mesh versus fabric, indexes, partitioning, CAP, and reverse engineering. Running the examples Every script in this guide runs on the public datalake-playground stack, which ships Spark 3.5.9 with the Iceberg runtime already on disk, and a PostgreSQL 16 container. Start it from its root: git clone https://github.com/rangareddy/datalake-playground.git cd datalake-playground SPARK_VERSION=3.5.9 sh run_datalake.sh start sh run_datalake.sh status The PySpark scripts use an Iceberg catalog named dm of type hadoop, whose warehouse is file:///tmp/dm_blog/warehouse inside the spark-master container. They never touch the shared Hive Metastore or MinIO buckets. Copy a script into the container and run it in local mode: docker cp scd_merge_demo.py spark-master:/tmp/ docker exec spark-master bash -c '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit \ --master "local[2]" \ --conf spark.eventLog.enabled=false \ --conf spark.ui.enabled=false \ --jars $(ls $ICEBERG_HOME/iceberg-spark-runtime*.jar) \ /tmp/scd_merge_demo.py' The SQL files run against a scratch database in the postgres container: docker exec postgres psql -U postgres -c 'CREATE DATABASE dm_blog' docker cp normalization.sql postgres:/tmp/ docker exec postgres psql -U postgres -d dm_blog -f /tmp/normalization.sql When you are done, remove both: docker exec spark-master rm -rf /tmp/dm_blog docker exec postgres psql -U postgres -c 'DROP DATABASE dm_blog' Part 1: Foundations of Data Modeling 1.1 What is data modeling, and why is it important? In plain terms. A data model is the agreement about what each table means, written down before anyone writes a query. A shop receipt shows it well: one receipt per purchase, one printed line per product. Anyone can total the receipt because everyone agrees what a line is. A model makes that agreement explicit for every table in the platform. A data model is not a diagram that happens to have tables on it. It is an executable agreement about what a row represents, what its keys identify, what time its attributes describe, and which operations are safe to perform on its measures. That agreement is what lets one team ingest changing operational data while another team builds reports without re-learning source-system quirks for every query. When the agreement is absent, SUM(order_total) may count an order once per line, a customer rename can rewrite historical sales, and a retry can double a batch. Those failures appear in dashboards, but their causes are in the model and load process. This guide uses an order-line sales process to connect the decisions that are usually taught separately: source events, grain, facts, dimensions, history, keys, quality checks, and lakehouse layout. The example is intentionally small; the rules are the same when the fact table has billions of rows. Without an explicit model, every downstream job has to rediscover entity identity, relationship cardinality, temporal meaning, and metric definitions. That spreads business rules into SQL notebooks and dashboards, where inconsistent copies are difficult to detect. Modeling makes those rules reviewable and testable at a shared boundary. It does not eliminate source quality problems; it tells the pipeline how to detect and represent them. A concrete failure. An orders table stores order_total on every line of the order, because the source export did. Order O1001 has two lines and a total of 35.00: order_id line_number product_id line_amount order_total O1001 1 P01 20.00 35.00 O1001 2 P02 15.00 35.00 SUM(line_amount) = 35.00 correct: line_amount belongs to the line SUM(order_total) = 70.00 wrong: order_total belongs to the order Nothing in the schema is invalid. The table simply mixes two grains, the order and the line, and one innocent SUM doubles revenue. Most of this guide is about preventing that class of error by design. 1.2 The three abstraction levels: conceptual, logical, and physical In plain terms. An architect draws a sketch of rooms first, then a floor plan with exact dimensions, then the construction drawings that say which bricks and pipes to use. Data models follow the same three steps. These levels answer different questions. Mixing them makes design reviews argue about implementation before agreeing on the business meaning. Conceptual model The conceptual model answers which business concepts exist and how they relate. Its artifact is an entity map or a domain model, drawn so a business owner can read it. In the sales example: customers place orders, orders contain lines, and products are sold. Logical model The logical model answers which attributes, keys, constraints, and cardinalities define the model. Its artifact is an ER model, a relational schema, or a dimensional model. In the sales example: one row per order line, with references to the customer, the product, and the date. Physical model The physical model answers how one specific engine stores and reads the model. Its artifacts are DDL, indexes, partitions, files, clustering, and distribution. In the sales example: PostgreSQL B-tree indexes, or Parquet files in an Iceberg table. The same logical model can be implemented as PostgreSQL tables, Spark DataFrames, or Iceberg tables. The logical relationships should survive a storage migration. Physical choices can change when access patterns or engine capabilities change; a customer identifier is not a good physical partition key merely because it is an important logical key. 1.3 Core building blocks: entities, attributes, relationships, and constraints In plain terms. Entities are the nouns (customer, product, order), attributes are their properties (email, price), relationships are the verbs (a customer places an order), and constraints are the rules (quantity must be positive). An entity is a distinguishable business object or event, such as a customer, product, order, or payment. An attribute records a property of that entity. A relationship records how entities associate. A constraint states which values and combinations are valid. For the order process, Customer and Product are entities; customer_id, email, and country_code are attributes; Customer places Order is a relationship. A constraint may state that an order-line quantity is positive or that (order_id, line_number) is unique. A model should distinguish a business fact from a convenient source-system column: a generated row number does not become a durable product identity just because it is unique in one extract. The data type is part of the attribute contract. A monetary measure needs a precision-preserving decimal and a currency policy; an event timestamp needs a time-zone interpretation; an identifier that may contain leading zeroes is usually text, not an integer. Types constrain values, but they do not capture all business rules. Use NOT NULL, uniqueness, foreign keys, checks, and pipeline assertions where the storage system can enforce them. Four type mistakes come up again and again: Postal codes stored as integers. postal_code = 02134 saved as an integer becomes 2134, and the leading zero cannot be recovered. Store postal codes as text. Money stored as floating point. unit_price = 0.10 as a float or double means 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, so totals drift by fractions of a cent. Use DECIMAL(10, 2) with a separate currency column. Timestamps without a time zone policy. An ordered_at value with no declared zone reads as two different days in two regions. Store a timestamp with a declared zone, such as UTC. Flags stored as free text. An is_active column holding 'Y', 'N', 'yes' and NULL gives three spellings of one value, and filters miss rows. Use a boolean with NOT NULL. 1.4 Identity management: primary keys, foreign keys, and alternate keys In plain terms. A key is how you point at exactly one thing. Your passport number is a business key, issued by someone else. The seat number on your boarding pass is closer to a surrogate key, assigned by the airline for this one trip. Primary key. Identifies one row in a relation. It is unique and non-null. Example: (order_id, line_number) on an order line. Foreign key. References a candidate key in another relation. Example: fact_order_line.product_sk -> dim_product.product_sk. Alternate key. A candidate identifier that was not chosen as the primary key. Example: a unique email within a defined identity scope. Business key. Identifies an entity in a source system or business process. Example: customer_id issued by the CRM. Surrogate key. A warehouse-controlled key for one model row or one version of it. Example: customer_sk = 102 for one Type 2 version of a customer. Do not assume these mechanisms have equal enforcement in every platform. PostgreSQL constraints can reject a row that violates a primary key, foreign key, or unique constraint. Many lakehouse engines store table schemas and metadata without enforcing the same cross-table foreign-key contract during every write. In that case, the pipeline must test referential integrity explicitly. Composite keys are not a modeling failure. They are often the honest source identity, such as (order_id, line_number). Surrogate keys are useful when source keys are unstable, multiple sources collide, or dimension history needs a distinct key per version. A surrogate key generated independently on every rebuild is not stable; preserve a key map or regenerate the facts that refer to it. Why both kinds exist. Two source systems can both use 1001 for different customers, and one customer can have two versions of history. Neither problem is solvable with the business key alone: source business key meaning warehouse surrogate key crm 1001 Ana Lopez customer_sk = 101 billing 1001 Raj Kumar (collision) customer_sk = 205 crm 1001 Ana Lopez, new segment customer_sk = 102 (version 2) 1.5 Understanding cardinality and modality In plain terms. Cardinality answers “how many?” and modality answers “is it required?” A customer can have zero or many orders; an order must have exactly one customer. Cardinality describes how many instances can participate in a relationship. Modality (also called optionality or minimum cardinality) describes whether participation is optional or required. Read a relationship by its minimum and maximum on both ends: Customer places Order. A customer has 0..many orders, and each order has exactly 1 customer. A customer may have no orders yet, but no order exists without a customer. Order contains Line. An order has 1..many lines, and each line belongs to exactly 1 order. A valid order has at least one line. Product appears on Line. A product appears on 0..many lines, and each line names exactly 1 product. A product may never have sold. ER diagrams draw the same rule with crow’s-foot notation. The symbol nearest an entity describes how many of that entity participate: CUSTOMER ||--------o< ORDER ||--------|< ORDER_LINE >o--------|| PRODUCT || exactly one o< zero or many |< one or many >o zero or many (drawn from the right) Read the first link from left to right as “one customer places zero or many orders”, and from right to left as “each order belongs to exactly one customer”. A many-to-many relationship usually needs an associative entity or bridge. For example, a sales line attributed to several campaigns cannot simply be joined to all campaigns and then summed: its amount is duplicated. Store the relationship at its own grain, then define whether queries filter through the bridge or allocate measures by weights. Section 2.2.2 runs that exact failure. 1.6 Types of data: structured, semi-structured, and unstructured In plain terms. A spreadsheet is structured, a JSON API response is semi-structured, and a scanned invoice PDF is unstructured. The less structure the data has, the more of its model you must add yourself. These terms describe how much organization is represented in the data, not whether it is important or valuable. Structured data has named fields with stable types and relationships. Model it by declaring columns, keys, nullability, and meaning explicitly. Semi-structured data is made of self-describing or nested records whose fields can vary, such as JSON events. Keep the source payload, project the governed fields into columns, and track schema versions. Unstructured data has no stable row-and-column schema: documents, images, audio. Store the object itself, and model its searchable metadata, identity, ownership, and lifecycle separately. JSON is not automatically a model, and Parquet is not automatically a good model. A nested payload may be the right raw representation for replay, while consumer-facing fields need explicit types, names, and evolution rules. A separate metadata row can model an image or document’s owner, classification, creation time, and object location without pretending its bytes are relational attributes. Part 1 interview questions 1. What is data modeling, and why does a data engineer need it rather than just a DBA? A data model is the agreed meaning of each dataset: what one row represents, which keys identify it, which time its attributes describe, and how its measures may be aggregated. Data engineers own the pipelines that create those rows, so they are the ones who either preserve that meaning or break it with a bad join, a blind append, or an untyped column. The DBA’s physical concerns, such as indexes and storage, come after the meaning is fixed. 2. Explain conceptual, logical, and physical models with one example. Conceptual: “customers place orders, orders contain lines”. Logical: order_line(order_id, line_number) is the primary key, customer_id is a required foreign key, and a customer has zero or many orders. Physical: an Iceberg table partitioned by days(order_ts), or a PostgreSQL table with a B-tree index on customer_id. The strongest answer adds that the physical level can change for performance without changing the logical meaning. 3. Business key vs surrogate key: why keep both? The business key (customer_id = C01) identifies the real-world entity and is how you match incoming source records. The surrogate key (customer_sk = 102) is owned by the warehouse and identifies one row or one historical version. You need the surrogate when sources collide on the same business key, when the business key can change, or when Type 2 history needs a distinct key for each version. Facts reference the surrogate so they point to the exact version that was true at the event time. 4. What is the difference between cardinality and modality? Cardinality is the maximum number of participants (one or many). Modality is the minimum (zero means optional, one means mandatory). “A customer has 0..many orders” is optional-many; “an order has exactly 1 customer” is mandatory-one. Modality decides whether a foreign key can be NULL and whether you need an “unknown” dimension member. 5. Why should money not be stored as a float? Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums of prices drift by small amounts and reconciliations fail. Use a fixed-point DECIMAL(p, s) and store the currency alongside it. In Spark, multiplying two decimals widens precision, so cast the result back to the declared contract type, as the fact-table demo in section 3.5 does. Part 2: Relational vs. Dimensional vs. Vault Modeling 2.1 Relational modeling: normalization (1NF-BCNF) vs. denormalization In plain terms. Normalization means storing each fact in exactly one place. If a city name is written on every order, renaming the city means editing thousands of rows, and missing one leaves the data contradicting itself. Normalization organizes a relational model to reduce update anomalies and inconsistent repetition. The normal forms are tests against a logical schema, not a contest to reach the largest possible number. First normal form (1NF) Each row-column position holds one value from the column’s domain, and repeating groups become related rows. It prevents columns such as phone_1, phone_2 and phone_3, which break the day a customer adds a fourth phone. Second normal form (2NF) The table is in 1NF, and every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not on part of it. It prevents a product name repeated on every (order_id, line_number) row when the name depends only on product_id. Third normal form (3NF) The table is in 2NF, and no non-key attribute depends on the key through another non-key attribute. It prevents customer_id -> postal_code -> city from being stored redundantly on every order. Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) For every nontrivial functional dependency X -> Y, X is a superkey. It catches determinants that are not candidate keys, which a schema can still have while meeting 3NF. The forms are stated with candidate keys and functional dependencies, not visual table aesthetics. BCNF is stricter than 3NF; decomposition can remove redundancy but may fail to preserve every dependency as a local constraint. Check whether the decomposed relations still enforce the business rules. The three anomalies normalization removes. Each one is a way for the data to contradict itself: Update anomaly. Renaming a city means editing every order row that repeats it. After 3NF, the city lives in one postal_area row. Insert anomaly. A new product cannot be stored until someone orders it. After 3NF, you insert into product alone. Delete anomaly. Deleting the only order for a product erases the product’s name. After 3NF, the product row exists independently of orders. Run it. normalization.sql builds the 3NF schema from the diagram with primary keys, foreign keys, and checks, then tries three bad inserts: -- One fact per place: customers, products, orders and order lines in 3NF. CREATE TABLE customer ( customer_id text PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL UNIQUE, postal_code text NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE postal_area ( postal_code text PRIMARY KEY, city text NOT NULL ); ALTER TABLE customer ADD FOREIGN KEY (postal_code) REFERENCES postal_area (postal_code); CREATE TABLE product ( product_id text PRIMARY KEY, product_name text NOT NULL, list_price numeric(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (list_price >= 0) ); CREATE TABLE sales_order ( order_id text PRIMARY KEY, customer_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES customer (customer_id), ordered_at timestamptz NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE order_line ( order_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES sales_order (order_id), line_number int NOT NULL, product_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES product (product_id), quantity int NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0), unit_price numeric(10, 2) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_number) ); INSERT INTO postal_area VALUES ('94105', 'San Francisco'), ('10001', 'New York'); INSERT INTO customer VALUES ('C01', 'ana@example.com', '94105'), ('C02', 'raj@example.com', '10001'); INSERT INTO product VALUES ('P01', 'Keyboard', 10.00), ('P02', 'Cable', 5.00); INSERT INTO sales_order VALUES ('O1001', 'C01', '2025-01-15 10:00:00+00'); INSERT INTO order_line VALUES ('O1001', 1, 'P01', 2, 10.00), ('O1001', 2, 'P02', 3, 5.00); -- The constraints reject bad rows instead of storing them. INSERT INTO order_line VALUES ('O1001', 3, 'P99', 1, 1.00); INSERT INTO order_line VALUES ('O1001', 1, 'P02', 1, 5.00); INSERT INTO order_line VALUES ('O1001', 4, 'P02', 0, 5.00); -- A city rename touches one row, not every order. UPDATE postal_area SET city = 'SF' WHERE postal_code = '94105'; SELECT o.order_id, l.line_number, c.customer_id, a.city, p.product_name, l.quantity * l.unit_price AS line_amount FROM order_line l JOIN sales_order o ON o.order_id = l.order_id JOIN customer c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN postal_area a ON a.postal_code = c.postal_code JOIN product p ON p.product_id = l.product_id ORDER BY l.line_number; PostgreSQL rejects each bad row with a named constraint, and the city rename updates one row: ERROR: insert or update on table "order_line" violates foreign key constraint "order_line_product_id_fkey" DETAIL: Key (product_id)=(P99) is not present in table "product". ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "order_line_pkey" DETAIL: Key (order_id, line_number)=(O1001, 1) already exists. ERROR: new row for relation "order_line" violates check constraint "order_line_quantity_check" DETAIL: Failing row contains (O1001, 4, P02, 0, 5.00). UPDATE 1 order_id | line_number | customer_id | city | product_name | line_amount ----------+-------------+-------------+------+--------------+------------- O1001 | 1 | C01 | SF | Keyboard | 20.00 O1001 | 2 | C01 | SF | Cable | 15.00 The price of that safety is visible in the final query: four joins to reassemble one order line. That cost is what the next technique trades away. Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes information to serve a read workload. It trades simpler or faster reads for extra write, storage, and consistency obligations. A star schema denormalizes descriptive attributes into dimensions, while its fact table remains narrow and keyed. That is not the same as copying every source field into one enormous table. Normalized (3NF) Denormalized (star, wide table) Optimized for Many small, concurrent writes (OLTP) Large scans and aggregations (OLAP) Each fact stored Once Possibly many times Joins per query Many Few Risk Slow analytical queries Inconsistent copies if the load process is wrong 2.2 Dimensional modeling core: fact tables vs. dimension tables In plain terms. A fact table records things that happened and can be counted or summed: an order line with its quantity and amount. Dimension tables describe the who, what, where and when you filter and group by: customer, product, date. Questions such as “revenue by product category by month” read as facts sliced by dimensions. Begin with a business event, not a target table. For sales, the source process might record an order with one or more product lines. A useful first statement is: One row in fact_order_line represents one product line accepted on one customer order. That sentence is the grain declaration. It names the real-world measurement event represented by one row. It is more useful than saying “the grain is order_id, line_number”: those columns may implement the grain, but the business sentence tells the team what the row means and which facts belong on it. Kimball’s guidance is to declare the grain before selecting dimensions or facts. Once grain is clear, the design follows: Operational events Analytical model ------------------- ---------------- orders + order lines -----------> fact_order_line customer change log -----------> dim_customer (versioned) product catalog -----------> dim_product calendar -----------> dim_date One accepted order line becomes one fact row. Each dimension key identifies the entity version relevant to that line. A fact table holds measurements of an event. Its columns are foreign keys to dimensions plus numeric measures, so it is narrow and very long, and every event adds a row. Example: fact_order_line(order_date_key, customer_sk, product_sk, quantity, net_amount). A dimension table holds descriptions of the things involved. Its columns are a surrogate key, a business key, and many text attributes, so it is wide and comparatively short. It grows only with new entities or new versions of them. Example: dim_product(product_sk, product_id, name, category, brand). The fact should contain measures that are true at this grain. For an order line, quantity, extended price, and line discount qualify. A customer lifetime total does not: it describes many orders and changes as more orders arrive. Store its derivation in the model or calculate it at query time, rather than repeating it on every line and making it additive by accident. Grain controls joins as well as measures. If a dimension join matches two rows for one order line, the join has changed the fact grain. Every measure then appears twice. A model that passes a schema check can still be wrong by a factor of two; uniqueness and join-cardinality checks are correctness tests. 2.2.1 Choose the fact-table shape The business process determines whether rows represent individual events, periodic states, or the progress of a workflow. Transaction fact. One row is one event, such as an accepted order line. It gives the most flexible drill-down and reconciliation. The cost is a large, sparse, append-oriented table, where corrections need an explicit policy. Periodic snapshot. One row is one entity at a regular interval, such as an account balance per day. It suits “as of” reporting and trend analysis. The table is predictably dense, and an unchanged balance is repeated every period. Accumulating snapshot. One row is one workflow instance, updated as each milestone lands: order fulfilment, insurance claims, loan applications. It makes lifecycle analysis easy. The cost is that a row is revisited, and the earlier milestone values have to be managed. These are modeling shapes, not storage formats. An Iceberg or Delta table can store any of them. A streaming pipeline can feed a transaction fact or update an accumulating snapshot; the table format does not decide what one row means. A fourth shape is worth knowing for interviews: the factless fact, which records that an event happened with no measure at all, such as a student attending a class. Its only “measure” is COUNT(*). 2.2.2 Choose a serving model for its consumers The staging model and the serving model need not have the same shape. Keep source-facing data faithful enough to replay and debug ingestion. Then publish a model whose joins, names, and measures match the questions consumers need to answer. Normalized relational model. Use it for operational writes and consistent entity updates. Analytical queries pay for it with more joins and need shared semantic rules. Dimensional star. Use it for BI filtering, grouping, and additive analysis. It requires a clear grain, conformed dimensions, and disciplined history handling. Data Vault. Use it for auditable integration of several changing sources. It needs more structures and transformations before analysts find it comfortable. One wide table. Use it for a narrow, stable workload or as a delivery boundary. It repeats attributes, makes history harder to express, and can multiply measures. These patterns can coexist in layers. A raw CDC landing table is not a star schema, and a medallion label such as “silver” does not define a grain. Decide what contract each layer provides, then materialize the serving model for its actual workload. Several dimension patterns change how a star model is queried without changing the fact grain: Conformed dimensions reuse the same definition and key domain across business processes, so sales and returns can be analyzed together. Role-playing dimensions use one logical dimension in multiple roles. An order fact may carry order_date_key, ship_date_key, and delivery_date_key, all referencing the date dimension. Degenerate dimensions keep a transaction identifier, such as order_id, on the fact when a separate dimension would contain little more than that identifier. Junk dimensions combine several low-cardinality flags, such as is_gift, payment_type and channel, into one small dimension of their combinations, instead of adding many tiny dimensions or many flag columns to the fact. Factless facts and bridge tables model events or many-to-many relationships without ordinary numeric measures. A bridge needs a filtering or allocation rule if joining it would repeat sales. Unknown and not-applicable members give missing references explicit keys. Do not collapse “not yet arrived,” “not collected,” “not applicable,” and “invalid source value” if they require different handling. Classify each measure before publishing it: Quantity sold is additive. It sums across order lines, products, and dates. Net line amount is additive, with conditions. Sum it when each line appears once and currency is handled: within one currency, or after conversion to a declared reporting currency. Unit price is non-additive. Recompute it as summed amount divided by summed quantity, or report a weighted measure. Never sum it. Account balance is semi-additive. It sums across accounts but not across time. Pick a defined closing or as-of balance; never add daily balances together. Margin percentage is a non-additive ratio. Recompute it from its additive numerator and denominator. Never average a ratio by averaging row-level percentages unless the business definition explicitly requires an unweighted average. Retain the additive components needed to derive unit price, conversion rates, and percentages. Run it. measures_demo.py puts the three classic measure traps side by side: summing a semi-additive balance, averaging a ratio, and joining through a bridge without weights. """Three measure traps: a semi-additive balance, a ratio, and a bridge table.""" from pyspark.sql import SparkSession spark = (SparkSession.builder .appName("measures-demo") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .getOrCreate()) # A periodic snapshot: one row per account per day. spark.createDataFrame([ ("A1", "2025-01-30", 100.0), ("A1", "2025-01-31", 120.0), ("A2", "2025-01-30", 50.0), ("A2", "2025-01-31", 40.0), ], "account_id string, snapshot_date string, balance double") \ .createOrReplaceTempView("fact_account_balance_daily") wrong_balance = spark.sql( "SELECT sum(balance) FROM fact_account_balance_daily").first()[0] closing_balance = spark.sql(""" SELECT sum(balance) FROM fact_account_balance_daily WHERE snapshot_date = (SELECT max(snapshot_date) FROM fact_account_balance_daily) """).first()[0] print("sum of daily balances:", wrong_balance, "| closing balance:", closing_balance) assert (wrong_balance, closing_balance) == (310.0, 160.0) # Margin %: averaging row-level ratios weights a 10.00 sale like a 1,000.00 sale. spark.createDataFrame([("L1", 1000.0, 100.0), ("L2", 10.0, 5.0)], "line_id string, revenue double, margin double") \ .createOrReplaceTempView("fact_sales") avg_of_ratios, ratio_of_sums = spark.sql(""" SELECT round(avg(margin / revenue) * 100, 2), round(sum(margin) / sum(revenue) * 100, 2) FROM fact_sales """).first() print("avg of row margins %:", avg_of_ratios, "| margin of totals %:", ratio_of_sums) assert (avg_of_ratios, ratio_of_sums) == (30.0, 10.4) # A bridge: order O1 is attributed to two campaigns with weights 0.7 and 0.3. spark.createDataFrame([("O1", 200.0), ("O2", 50.0)], "order_id string, net_amount double") \ .createOrReplaceTempView("fact_order") spark.createDataFrame([("O1", "EMAIL", 0.7), ("O1", "SEARCH", 0.3), ("O2", "SEARCH", 1.0)], "order_id string, campaign string, weight double") \ .createOrReplaceTempView("bridge_order_campaign") naive, allocated = spark.sql(""" SELECT sum(f.net_amount), round(sum(f.net_amount * b.weight), 2) FROM fact_order f JOIN bridge_order_campaign b ON f.order_id = b.order_id """).first() print("revenue through bridge, naive:", naive, "| allocated:", allocated) assert (naive, allocated) == (450.0, 250.0) # The invariant that makes allocation safe: weights sum to 1 per order. bad_weights = spark.sql(""" SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT order_id FROM bridge_order_campaign GROUP BY order_id HAVING abs(sum(weight) - 1) > 1e-9) """).first()[0] assert bad_weights == 0 print("PASS: closing balance 160, margin 10.4%, allocated revenue 250") spark.stop() sum of daily balances: 310.0 | closing balance: 160.0 avg of row margins %: 30.0 | margin of totals %: 10.4 revenue through bridge, naive: 450.0 | allocated: 250.0 PASS: closing balance 160, margin 10.4%, allocated revenue 250 All three wrong answers come from valid SQL. Summing two days of balances counts the same money twice. Averaging row margins lets a 10.00 sale weigh as much as a 1,000.00 sale, giving 30% where the business margin is 10.4%. The naive bridge join repeats order O1’s 200.00 once per campaign, reporting 450.00 of revenue for 250.00 of orders. The fix in each case is a modeling rule, not a faster engine. 2.3 Schema topologies: star schema vs. snowflake schema In plain terms. In a star schema the fact table sits in the middle and every dimension is one join away, like spokes on a wheel. A snowflake splits some dimensions into further tables (product, then subcategory, then category), so the drawing branches like a snowflake. A star schema connects a fact directly to descriptive dimensions. A snowflake schema normalizes some dimension attributes into additional related tables. The difference is dimension topology, not fact grain. Star. The typical form is fact_sales -> dim_product(category, subcategory, ...). It gives fewer joins and a compact semantic surface for common analysis. The cost is repeated descriptions across product rows, so an attribute update touches more rows. Snowflake. The typical form is fact_sales -> dim_product -> dim_subcategory -> dim_category. Hierarchy values are shared and dimension storage is less duplicated. The cost is more joins, more relationship paths, and more chances for confusing filter behavior. Do not normalize a dimension merely because the source is normalized, and do not flatten every hierarchy automatically. Choose the form that makes the consumer contract understandable and can meet measured query and update requirements. A large, shared hierarchy with independently governed attributes may justify snowflaking; a small presentation dimension often benefits more from a direct star join. A third topology, the galaxy or fact constellation, is several fact tables sharing conformed dimensions: fact_order_line and fact_return_line both join dim_product and dim_date, which is what makes “returns as a share of sales by category” a valid query. 2.4 Data Vault 2.0: hubs, links, and satellites In plain terms. Data Vault stores three things separately: the list of business keys that exist (hubs), which keys are connected (links), and every version of the descriptive details (satellites). Because each piece only ever grows, you can load from many sources at once and still audit exactly what arrived and when. Data Vault separates durable business identity, relationships, and changing descriptions into different structures. A hub records a business key; a link records an association between hubs; a satellite records descriptive attributes and their history for a hub or link. Load time and source lineage are commonly retained so integrations can be audited. This separation can help when multiple sources contribute changing records and the integration history must remain available. It also introduces more joins and more structures than most analysts should query directly. A common architecture uses a Vault as an integration/history layer and publishes star schemas as marts for reporting. Hash keys are a common implementation choice, not a substitute for canonicalizing business keys, testing collisions, or maintaining source identity. Run it. data_vault_demo.py loads a hub and a satellite twice from two sources. The same customer arrives as " c01 " and as "C01", and the second load changes only one customer: """Load a Data Vault hub, link and satellite from two sources, twice. Hash keys come from the canonicalized business key; the satellite only gains a row when the hash of its descriptive attributes changes. """ from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F spark = (SparkSession.builder .appName("data-vault-demo") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC") .getOrCreate()) def hash_key(*cols): """SHA-256 over trimmed, upper-cased parts joined by a delimiter.""" return F.sha2(F.concat_ws("||", *[F.upper(F.trim(F.col(c))) for c in cols]), 256) def stage(df, source, load_ts): return (df .withColumn("hk_customer", hash_key("customer_id")) .withColumn("hashdiff", F.sha2(F.concat_ws("||", F.coalesce(F.col("email"), F.lit("")), F.coalesce(F.col("segment"), F.lit(""))), 256)) .withColumn("record_source", F.lit(source)) .withColumn("load_ts", F.to_timestamp(F.lit(load_ts)))) hub = spark.createDataFrame([], "hk_customer string, customer_id string, " "record_source string, load_ts timestamp") sat = spark.createDataFrame([], "hk_customer string, hashdiff string, email string, " "segment string, record_source string, load_ts timestamp") def load(hub, sat, staged): # Hub: insert business keys never seen before, from any source. new_keys = (staged .select("hk_customer", F.upper(F.trim("customer_id")).alias("customer_id"), "record_source", "load_ts") .dropDuplicates(["hk_customer"]) .join(hub.select("hk_customer"), "hk_customer", "left_anti")) hub = hub.unionByName(new_keys) # Satellite: insert only when the latest stored hashdiff differs. latest = (sat.groupBy("hk_customer").agg( F.max_by("hashdiff", "load_ts").alias("last_hashdiff"))) changed = (staged.join(latest, "hk_customer", "left") .filter(F.col("last_hashdiff").isNull() | (F.col("last_hashdiff") != F.col("hashdiff"))) .select(sat.columns)) return hub, sat.unionByName(changed) crm_day1 = spark.createDataFrame( [(" c01 ", "ana@example.com", "Gold"), ("C02", "raj@example.com", "Silver")], "customer_id string, email string, segment string") hub, sat = load(hub, sat, stage(crm_day1, "crm", "2025-01-01 02:00:00")) # Day 2: C01 arrives again from the web shop in a different spelling and with # a new segment; C02 is unchanged. crm_day2 = spark.createDataFrame( [("C01", "ana@example.com", "Silver"), ("C02", "raj@example.com", "Silver")], "customer_id string, email string, segment string") hub, sat = load(hub, sat, stage(crm_day2, "web", "2025-01-02 02:00:00")) hub.select(F.substring("hk_customer", 1, 12).alias("hk_customer"), "customer_id", "record_source").orderBy("customer_id").show() sat.select(F.substring("hk_customer", 1, 12).alias("hk_customer"), "segment", "record_source", F.col("load_ts").cast("date").alias("load_date")) \ .orderBy("hk_customer", "load_ts").show() assert hub.count() == 2 # " c01 " and "C01" are one customer assert sat.count() == 3 # C01 twice, C02 once: no duplicate for C02 # A link records an association between hubs, here order -> customer. orders = spark.createDataFrame([("O1001", "C01"), ("O1002", " c01")], "order_id string, customer_id string") link = (orders .withColumn("hk_order", hash_key("order_id")) .withColumn("hk_customer", hash_key("customer_id")) .withColumn("hk_order_customer", hash_key("order_id", "customer_id")) .select("hk_order_customer", "hk_order", "hk_customer")) assert link.join(hub, "hk_customer").count() == 2 print("PASS: hub 2 keys, satellite 3 versions, link resolves to the hub") spark.stop() +------------+-----------+-------------+ | hk_customer|customer_id|record_source| +------------+-----------+-------------+ |132bfbedb168| C01| crm| |371e0b6ba48a| C02| crm| +------------+-----------+-------------+ +------------+-------+-------------+----------+ | hk_customer|segment|record_source| load_date| +------------+-------+-------------+----------+ |132bfbedb168| Gold| crm|2025-01-01| |132bfbedb168| Silver| web|2025-01-02| |371e0b6ba48a| Silver| crm|2025-01-01| +------------+-------+-------------+----------+ PASS: hub 2 keys, satellite 3 versions, link resolves to the hub Three behaviours to take from the output. Trimming and upper-casing before hashing makes both spellings of C01 produce one hub row; skip that step and the vault quietly holds two customers. The hub keeps the source that first delivered the key, while each satellite row records its own source. And C02, unchanged on day 2, gets no new satellite row, because its hashdiff matched the latest stored one. Kimball star Data Vault 3NF (Inmon) warehouse Primary goal Fast, understandable analysis Auditable integration of many sources One normalized enterprise model History SCD types on dimensions Every satellite row, insert-only Effective dates on entities Loading Transform, then load Insert-only, highly parallel Transform into the enterprise model Query by analysts Directly Usually through marts Usually through marts Part 2 interview questions 1. Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with one example. Start from an order row that lists several products in one cell. 1NF: one value per cell, so each product becomes its own row keyed by (order_id, line_number). 2NF: product_name depends only on product_id, which is part of the key, so move it to a product table. 3NF: city depends on postal_code, not on the key, so move it to a postal_area table. Mention the anomaly each step removes: a city rename then updates one row instead of every order. 2. When would you denormalize? When the workload is read-heavy and join-heavy, as in analytics, and the duplicated attributes can be kept consistent by a controlled load process. A star schema is deliberate denormalization of dimensions. Do not denormalize a transactional system that takes many concurrent updates, because every copy becomes a place where the data can disagree. 3. What is grain, and why is it declared first? Grain is what one row of a fact table represents, written as a business sentence: “one row per product line on an accepted order”. It is declared first because it decides which measures are valid on the row and which dimension joins are safe. A join that matches two rows per fact changes the grain and doubles every measure. 4. Additive, semi-additive, and non-additive measures: give an example of each. Additive: quantity sold, which sums across every dimension. Semi-additive: account balance or inventory on hand, which sums across accounts but not across time; take the closing value per period instead. Non-additive: unit price or margin percentage; store the numerator and denominator and divide after summing. In the demo, averaging row margins gave 30% while the true margin was 10.4%. 5. Star vs snowflake: which would you choose? Default to a star: fewer joins, simpler SQL for analysts, and BI tools handle it well. Snowflake a dimension when a hierarchy is large, shared by several dimensions, and governed separately, or when the storage saved by not repeating its values matters. The fact grain is the same either way. 6. What are conformed, role-playing, degenerate and junk dimensions? Conformed: one dimension with the same keys and meaning, shared by several facts, so sales and returns can be compared. Role-playing: one dimension used in several roles, such as dim_date as order date, ship date and delivery date. Degenerate: a transaction ID such as order_id kept on the fact with no dimension table. Junk: one small dimension that holds the combinations of several low-cardinality flags. 7. What are hubs, links and satellites, and why hash the business key? A hub stores each unique business key once. A link stores a relationship between hubs. A satellite stores descriptive attributes with load time and source, and gets a new row only when the attributes change, detected by comparing a hashdiff. Hashing the canonicalized business key gives a deterministic key that any loader can compute independently, so hubs, links and satellites load in parallel without looking up a sequence. Canonicalize first: trim and upper-case, or " c01 " and "C01" become two customers. 8. How do you handle a many-to-many relationship between a fact and a dimension? Use a bridge table at the grain of the relationship, such as (order_id, campaign). Then either filter through it (“orders that touched the EMAIL campaign”) without summing, or store allocation weights that sum to 1 per fact and multiply the measure by the weight. Test the sum-to-one invariant. A plain join repeats the measure once per related row. Part 3: Advanced Data Engineering Concepts & Storage Patterns Part 2 defined the serving model. This part follows how that model changes as source data arrives, business attributes evolve, and storage formats change. dim_date | dim_customer ---- fact_order_line ---- dim_product | dim_channel fact_order_line grain: one row per order_id + line_number Measures: quantity, gross_amount, discount_amount 3.1 Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Types 0–6 Deep Dive) In plain terms. Customers move, products get renamed, sales reps change territory. An SCD type is the rule for what happens to history when a dimension attribute changes: forget the old value, keep it in a new row, or keep it in an extra column. The SCD number is a response policy for changed attributes, not a property of the whole dimension table. Apply policies at the attribute level. Type 2 is the workhorse when historical facts must retain the dimension values that were true when the event occurred; other types fit distinct questions. This guide follows Kimball’s named patterns. Type numbers beyond 1–3 are not used consistently by every vendor or author, so document the chosen behavior instead of relying on a number alone. Type 0: retain the original The first accepted value never changes. Use it when the original value is durable by definition, or explicitly labeled “original”, such as original_signup_channel. Type 1: overwrite Only the latest value is kept. Use it to correct an error, or when the business intentionally restates all history with the new value. Type 2: add a row Each effective version gets its own row and its own surrogate key. Use it when historical facts must resolve to the attribute version that was valid at event time. This is the type interviews ask about most. Type 3: add a column The row keeps the current value plus one or a few prior values in extra columns. Use it when a limited comparison, such as current region versus previous region, is enough. Type 4: mini-dimension Volatile attributes move to a separate dimension of attribute profiles. Use it when several attributes change rapidly, or their combinations would explode the base dimension. Type 5: mini-dimension plus a current pointer Type 4 profile history, plus a Type 1 reference to the current profile on the base dimension. Use it when facts need the historical profile and consumers also want easy access to the current one. Type 6: hybrid of Types 1, 2 and 3 Version rows, plus current-value columns overwritten on every historical row. Use it when consumers need both “as was” and “as is” reporting without a separate current-key join. The same change under four types. Customer C01 moves from Gold to Silver on 1 February. This is what dim_customer holds afterwards: Type 0 (keep original) customer_sk customer_id segment 101 C01 Gold <- the change is ignored Type 1 (overwrite) customer_sk customer_id segment 101 C01 Silver <- January sales now report as Silver Type 2 (new row) customer_sk customer_id segment valid_from valid_to is_current 101 C01 Gold 2025-01-01 2025-02-01 false 102 C01 Silver 2025-02-01 9999-12-31 true Type 3 (new column) customer_sk customer_id segment previous_segment 101 C01 Silver Gold <- one step of history Types 5 and 6 duplicate or update information to make current-state questions easier. That convenience creates maintenance work: every affected Type 6 version row must receive the current overlay, and a Type 5 current pointer must be updated when the profile changes. If that synchronization is late, “current” attributes become stale while the Type 2 history may still be correct. Keep business identity separate from warehouse identity A business key comes from the source domain: customer_id = C01 identifies the customer across source updates. A surrogate key is assigned by the warehouse to identify one dimension row or version, for example customer_sk = 101 for the customer’s Gold version and customer_sk = 102 for the later Silver version. The fact normally stores the surrogate key. If the customer changes segment, the current source key remains C01, but the new dimension version receives a new surrogate key. This preserves both identity and history. A generated surrogate key must be stable across incremental runs; monotonically_increasing_id() and an unpersisted row_number() are not durable key-assignment strategies. Use a persisted key map or the warehouse platform’s governed key-generation process. Composite business keys are valid when they describe source identity. If a source identifies an order line with (order_id, line_number), do not discard one part and hope the remaining ID is unique. Preserve the components or map them to a stable key, and test uniqueness at the declared grain. Type 2: make dimension history explicit For Type 2, model a half-open validity interval [valid_from, valid_to). The old version is valid at its start and stops being valid exactly when the next version starts. Half-open intervals avoid double matches at a boundary: customer_id customer_sk segment valid_from valid_to C01 101 Gold 2025-01-01 00:00:00 2025-02-01 00:00:00 C01 102 Silver 2025-02-01 00:00:00 9999-12-31 00:00:00 To attach the right customer to a sale, match both the business key and event time: o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_ts >= c.valid_from AND o.order_ts < c.valid_to Joining on customer_id alone can match every historical version and multiply the sale. Joining only to the current row keeps one result but restates old sales using today’s attributes. Neither is a harmless implementation choice; they answer different business questions. Run it: SCD Type 1 and Type 2 with Iceberg MERGE. A Type 2 load has to do two things for each changed customer in one atomic step: close the current version and insert the new one. A single MERGE can only take one action per source row, so the standard trick stages each changed customer twice. One copy carries the real key and matches the current version, which gets closed. The other copy carries a NULL merge key, matches nothing, and is inserted as the new version. scd_merge_demo.py does that, then applies a Type 1 overwrite of email across all versions, then runs the point-in-time join: """SCD Type 1 and Type 2 on an Iceberg dimension, then a point-in-time fact join. Runs on datalake-playground's spark-master in local mode. The Iceberg catalog is a Hadoop catalog on the container's local disk, so nothing touches the shared metastore or MinIO. """ from pyspark.sql import SparkSession spark = (SparkSession.builder .appName("scd-merge-demo") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm.type", "hadoop") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm.warehouse", "file:///tmp/dm_blog/warehouse") .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC") .getOrCreate()) spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS dm.sales") spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dm.sales.dim_customer PURGE") spark.sql(""" CREATE TABLE dm.sales.dim_customer ( customer_sk BIGINT NOT NULL, customer_id STRING NOT NULL, email STRING, segment STRING, valid_from TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, valid_to TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, is_current BOOLEAN NOT NULL ) USING iceberg """) # Initial load: three customers, all valid from 1 January. spark.sql(""" INSERT INTO dm.sales.dim_customer VALUES (101, 'C01', 'ana@example.com', 'Gold', TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31', true), (201, 'C02', 'raj@example.com', 'Silver', TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31', true), (301, 'C03', 'li@example.com', 'Bronze', TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31', true) """) # The 1 February batch: C01 changes segment (Type 2), C02 changes only its # email (Type 1), C03 is unchanged, and C04 is new. spark.createDataFrame( [("C01", "ana@example.com", "Silver", "2025-02-01 00:00:00"), ("C02", "raj.k@example.com", "Silver", "2025-02-01 00:00:00"), ("C03", "li@example.com", "Bronze", "2025-02-01 00:00:00"), ("C04", "sam@example.com", "Gold", "2025-02-01 00:00:00")], "customer_id string, email string, segment string, effective_from string", ).selectExpr("*", "CAST(effective_from AS TIMESTAMP) AS effective_ts") \ .createOrReplaceTempView("customer_updates") # New surrogate keys come from the table's current maximum, so a key, once # written, never changes on a later run. spark.sql(""" CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW staged AS WITH changed AS ( SELECT u.* FROM customer_updates u LEFT JOIN dm.sales.dim_customer d ON d.customer_id = u.customer_id AND d.is_current WHERE d.customer_id IS NULL OR d.segment <> u.segment ), keyed AS ( SELECT c.*, (SELECT max(customer_sk) FROM dm.sales.dim_customer) + row_number() OVER (ORDER BY c.customer_id) AS new_sk FROM changed c ) -- Row 1 per change: matches the current version and closes it. SELECT customer_id AS merge_key, * FROM keyed UNION ALL -- Row 2 per change: matches nothing, so it inserts the new version. SELECT NULL AS merge_key, * FROM keyed """) # Type 2: close the old version and open a new one. spark.sql(""" MERGE INTO dm.sales.dim_customer t USING staged s ON t.customer_id = s.merge_key AND t.is_current WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.valid_to = s.effective_ts, t.is_current = false WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.merge_key IS NULL THEN INSERT (customer_sk, customer_id, email, segment, valid_from, valid_to, is_current) VALUES (s.new_sk, s.customer_id, s.email, s.segment, s.effective_ts, TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31', true) """) # Type 1: overwrite email on every version of the customer, history included. spark.sql(""" MERGE INTO dm.sales.dim_customer t USING customer_updates u ON t.customer_id = u.customer_id WHEN MATCHED AND t.email <> u.email THEN UPDATE SET t.email = u.email """) dim = spark.sql(""" SELECT customer_sk, customer_id, email, segment, CAST(valid_from AS DATE) AS valid_from, CAST(valid_to AS DATE) AS valid_to, is_current FROM dm.sales.dim_customer ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from """) dim.show(truncate=False) rows = {r.customer_sk: r for r in dim.collect()} assert len(rows) == 5 assert not rows[101].is_current and str(rows[101].valid_to) == "2025-02-01" assert rows[302].customer_id == "C01" and rows[302].segment == "Silver" assert rows[303].customer_id == "C04" assert rows[201].email == "raj.k@example.com" and rows[201].is_current # Validity intervals for one customer never overlap. overlaps = spark.sql(""" SELECT count(*) FROM dm.sales.dim_customer a JOIN dm.sales.dim_customer b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id AND a.customer_sk < b.customer_sk AND a.valid_from < b.valid_to AND b.valid_from < a.valid_to """).first()[0] assert overlaps == 0 # Point-in-time join: each order picks the version valid when it happened. spark.createDataFrame( [("O1001", "C01", "2025-01-15 10:00:00", 20.00), ("O1002", "C01", "2025-02-10 11:00:00", 9.00)], "order_id string, customer_id string, ordered_at string, net_amount double", ).selectExpr("*", "CAST(ordered_at AS TIMESTAMP) AS order_ts") \ .createOrReplaceTempView("orders") point_in_time = spark.sql(""" SELECT o.order_id, d.customer_sk, d.segment AS segment_at_order, o.net_amount FROM orders o JOIN dm.sales.dim_customer d ON o.customer_id = d.customer_id AND o.order_ts >= d.valid_from AND o.order_ts < d.valid_to ORDER BY o.order_id """) point_in_time.show() assert [r.segment_at_order for r in point_in_time.collect()] == ["Gold", "Silver"] # The tempting join on customer_id alone doubles every C01 order. wrong = spark.sql(""" SELECT count(*) AS joined_rows, sum(o.net_amount) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN dm.sales.dim_customer d ON o.customer_id = d.customer_id """).first() print("customer_id-only join:", wrong.joined_rows, "rows, revenue", wrong.revenue) assert wrong.joined_rows == 4 and wrong.revenue == 58.0 spark.sql("SELECT operation " "FROM dm.sales.dim_customer.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at").show() print("PASS: 5 customer versions, no overlaps, point-in-time join correct") spark.stop() +-----------+-----------+-----------------+-------+----------+----------+----------+ |customer_sk|customer_id|email |segment|valid_from|valid_to |is_current| +-----------+-----------+-----------------+-------+----------+----------+----------+ |101 |C01 |ana@example.com |Gold |2025-01-01|2025-02-01|false | |302 |C01 |ana@example.com |Silver |2025-02-01|9999-12-31|true | |201 |C02 |raj.k@example.com|Silver |2025-01-01|9999-12-31|true | |301 |C03 |li@example.com |Bronze |2025-01-01|9999-12-31|true | |303 |C04 |sam@example.com |Gold |2025-02-01|9999-12-31|true | +-----------+-----------+-----------------+-------+----------+----------+----------+ +--------+-----------+----------------+----------+ |order_id|customer_sk|segment_at_order|net_amount| +--------+-----------+----------------+----------+ | O1001| 101| Gold| 20.0| | O1002| 302| Silver| 9.0| +--------+-----------+----------------+----------+ customer_id-only join: 4 rows, revenue 58.0 +---------+ |operation| +---------+ | append| |overwrite| |overwrite| +---------+ PASS: 5 customer versions, no overlaps, point-in-time join correct Read the result row by row. C01 changed segment, so version 101 was closed at 1 February and version 302 opened. C02 changed only its email, a Type 1 attribute, so it was overwritten in place with no new version. C03 was unchanged and untouched. C04 was new and got its first version. New surrogate keys continue from the table’s maximum (301), so keys already written never change on a rerun. Each MERGE committed as one Iceberg snapshot (overwrite), so a reader never sees a closed version without its replacement. The final check is the one that matters for reports: the point-in-time join returns two rows and 29.00, while the customer_id-only join returns four rows and 58.00 with no error. 3.2 Change Data Capture (CDC): mechanics and design patterns In plain terms. Instead of copying a whole table every night, CDC reads the database’s own change journal and ships only what changed: this row was inserted, that one updated, this one deleted. The hard part is not capturing the changes; it is applying them in the right order, exactly once in effect. Change Data Capture records changes at the source boundary so downstream systems can maintain a copy without repeatedly scanning the entire source. There are three common capture paths: Log-based CDC reads the database transaction log or WAL. The operational concerns are log retention, replication slots, privileges, and source-specific ordering. Trigger-based CDC reads changes that database triggers write to an outbox or audit table. The concerns are trigger overhead, transaction behavior, and cleanup of the capture table. Query-based CDC polls periodically with a timestamp or a monotonically increasing key. Deletes and intermediate updates can be invisible, and timestamps can arrive late or be non-unique. Log-based CDC is not simply “a stream of row JSON.” A Debezium event can include a key, before/after values, operation type, source metadata and log position. A connector may first emit a consistent snapshot, then continue from the corresponding log position. Consumers must distinguish snapshot reads from inserts, updates, deletes, and tombstones, and must use the source’s ordering metadata rather than a connector processing timestamp when ordering matters. Source transaction log | v CDC connector: snapshot + ordered change events | v Immutable landing log: key, op, source position, event time, payload | v Deduplicate and order -> current-state tables / SCDs / facts The raw event log and the analytical model answer different questions. The event log is useful for replay and audit. A current-state table applies the latest accepted operation per key. A Type 2 dimension turns selected attribute changes into effective versions. A transaction fact records business events at their declared grain. Do not interpret every update as a new business event, or every delete as a physical row removal. Define how the consumer handles at-least-once delivery: retain a source position such as an LSN or log offset, use a stable row key and deterministic ordering, make replays idempotent, and test duplicate delivery. A primary-key change may be represented as deletion of the old key plus insertion of the new key. A source snapshot can also overlap the live stream unless the connector’s snapshot protocol resolves that boundary. The pipeline’s idempotency and ordering rules must cover both cases. CDC application patterns Append-only event fact: keep each distinct business event and deduplicate by event identity. Preserve correction events instead of silently rewriting a prior event when the business requires an audit trail. Current-state upsert: group changes by business key and apply them in source order. A delete becomes a tombstone or explicit deleted state if downstream consumers need to know that the key existed. Type 2 history: compare tracked attributes, expire the current version, and insert a new version with effective-time boundaries. Snapshot plus stream: bootstrap from a consistent snapshot and continue from its source-log boundary. Reconciliation compares the snapshot’s key set and values with the resulting target state. CDC does not provide free exactly-once business effects. A sink may commit a row while the offset commit fails, causing a replay. Coordinate the sink transaction and offset where supported; otherwise use idempotent writes and durable source positions. Run it: apply CDC idempotently. cdc_apply_demo.py takes seven Debezium-style events for three customers, including a snapshot, two updates to one key, a delete, an insert, and one redelivered event. It then replays the batch, sends a late older event, and finally shows the trap that hard deletes create: """Apply a batch of Debezium-style change events to an Iceberg current-state table. The batch contains a snapshot, two updates to one key, a delete, an insert and a redelivered event. Applying it twice must leave the table unchanged. """ from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, Window, functions as F spark = (SparkSession.builder .appName("cdc-apply-demo") .config("spark.sql.extensions", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm.type", "hadoop") .config("spark.sql.catalog.dm.warehouse", "file:///tmp/dm_blog/warehouse") .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "UTC") .getOrCreate()) spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS dm.sales") spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dm.sales.customer_current PURGE") spark.sql(""" CREATE TABLE dm.sales.customer_current ( customer_id STRING NOT NULL, email STRING, segment STRING, source_lsn BIGINT NOT NULL ) USING iceberg """) # op: r = snapshot read, c = create, u = update, d = delete. # lsn is the source log position; it, not arrival order, decides which wins. events = spark.createDataFrame([ ("r", 1, "C01", "ana@example.com", "Gold"), ("r", 2, "C02", "raj@example.com", "Silver"), ("u", 10, "C01", "ana@example.com", "Silver"), ("d", 11, "C02", None, None), ("u", 12, "C01", "ana.m@example.com", "Silver"), ("c", 13, "C05", "kim@example.com", "Bronze"), ("u", 12, "C01", "ana.m@example.com", "Silver"), # redelivered ], "op string, lsn bigint, customer_id string, email string, segment string") # Keep the latest event per key. Exact redeliveries collapse first. latest = (events .dropDuplicates(["customer_id", "lsn"]) .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over( Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("lsn").desc()))) .filter("rn = 1") .drop("rn")) latest.orderBy("customer_id").show() latest.createOrReplaceTempView("latest_changes") apply_sql = """ MERGE INTO dm.sales.customer_current t USING latest_changes s ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'd' AND s.lsn > t.source_lsn THEN DELETE WHEN MATCHED AND s.op <> 'd' AND s.lsn > t.source_lsn THEN UPDATE SET t.email = s.email, t.segment = s.segment, t.source_lsn = s.lsn WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'd' THEN INSERT (customer_id, email, segment, source_lsn) VALUES (s.customer_id, s.email, s.segment, s.lsn) """ spark.sql(apply_sql) first = spark.table("dm.sales.customer_current").orderBy("customer_id") first.show() first_rows = [tuple(r) for r in first.collect()] assert first_rows == [("C01", "ana.m@example.com", "Silver", 12), ("C05", "kim@example.com", "Bronze", 13)] # Replay the same batch, as an at-least-once consumer will after a crash. spark.sql(apply_sql) replayed = [tuple(r) for r in spark.table("dm.sales.customer_current").orderBy("customer_id").collect()] assert replayed == first_rows # An older event arriving late must not overwrite a newer one. spark.createDataFrame([("u", 10, "C01", "ana@example.com", "Silver")], events.schema).createOrReplaceTempView("latest_changes") spark.sql(apply_sql) assert spark.table("dm.sales.customer_current") \ .filter("customer_id = 'C01'").first().source_lsn == 12 # The trap: C02 was hard-deleted, so the target no longer remembers lsn 11. # A late update older than the delete now looks like a brand-new key. spark.createDataFrame([("u", 2, "C02", "raj@example.com", "Silver")], events.schema).createOrReplaceTempView("latest_changes") spark.sql(apply_sql) resurrected = spark.table("dm.sales.customer_current") \ .filter("customer_id = 'C02'").count() print("C02 rows after a late pre-delete event:", resurrected) assert resurrected == 1 print("PASS: 7 events -> 2 rows; replay and late update were no-ops; " "late event after a hard delete resurrected C02") spark.stop() +---+---+-----------+-----------------+-------+ | op|lsn|customer_id| email|segment| +---+---+-----------+-----------------+-------+ | u| 12| C01|ana.m@example.com| Silver| | d| 11| C02| NULL| NULL| | c| 13| C05| kim@example.com| Bronze| +---+---+-----------+-----------------+-------+ +-----------+-----------------+-------+----------+ |customer_id| email|segment|source_lsn| +-----------+-----------------+-------+----------+ | C01|ana.m@example.com| Silver| 12| | C05| kim@example.com| Bronze| 13| +-----------+-----------------+-------+----------+ C02 rows after a late pre-delete event: 1 PASS: 7 events -> 2 rows; replay and late update were no-ops; late event after a hard delete resurrected C02 Three guards make the apply idempotent. Exact redeliveries collapse on (customer_id, lsn). Only the highest lsn per key survives, so the intermediate update at lsn = 10 is never written. Every MATCHED branch requires s.lsn > t.source_lsn, so a replay or an older straggler changes nothing. The last step shows what those guards cannot protect. Once C02 is physically deleted, the target has no row left to remember that lsn = 11 was its last change. A late event at lsn = 2 arrives, hits NOT MATCHED, and inserts the customer again. If late or out-of-order delivery is possible, keep a tombstone (is_deleted = true plus the delete’s lsn) instead of removing the row, and purge tombstones only after the maximum lateness window has passed. 3.3 Storage evolution: warehouses vs. data lakes vs. data lakehouses In plain terms. A warehouse is a managed database tuned for SQL analytics. A lake is cheap file storage that holds anything. A lakehouse adds a table format such as Iceberg on top of the lake’s files, so many engines can share tables with transactions, schemas, and snapshots. These names describe broad storage and access patterns, not one required product or modeling method. Data warehouse. It provides managed SQL tables, transaction processing, catalogs, and query optimization. Curated schemas and constraints sit close to the serving engine. What it does not give you by itself is agreement on metric meaning or source history. Data lake. It provides low-cost files and object storage for varied data and compute engines. Raw, semi-structured, and curated data can coexist, so contracts need explicit owners. Storing Parquet files does not give you atomic table transactions. Data lakehouse. It provides lake storage plus an open table format and a metadata and catalog layer. Several engines can share schemas, snapshots, and table-level commits. It still does not give you every relational constraint, cross-table transactions, or semantic definitions. Parquet is a file format. Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Hudi add table metadata and commit behavior around data files; they do not make the data model correct. Table-level atomicity is also not automatically a transaction spanning several tables. If a fact and dimension publish in separate commits, define how consumers identify a compatible model version or batch. Medallion architecture: bronze, silver, and gold Medallion architecture is a way to organize a lakehouse’s data lifecycle into progressively more validated and purpose-shaped layers. It is a logical pattern, not a different fact-table design, a particular file format, or a requirement that every transformation create another physical table. The bronze/silver/gold labels also do not define row grain; each table still needs its own contract. Bronze preserves the source. It keeps source-shaped records and ingestion metadata for replay and audit. In the sales example, that is the raw order CDC envelope with key, operation, source position, and before/after payload. Keep source identity, capture time, source event time, and schema version explicit. Silver cleans the detail. It validates, types, deduplicates, and standardizes detailed records: curated order lines and customer change history with normalized timestamps and currencies. Keep business keys, source ordering, invalid-row handling, and Type 2 effective-time rules explicit. Gold publishes the contract. It holds business-facing dimensional models and workload-specific aggregates: fact_order_line, dim_customer, dim_product, and sales summaries. Keep the declared grain, conformed dimensions, measure definitions, freshness, and consumer contract explicit. CDC snapshot + change log | v bronze.order_events source-faithful, replayable | v silver.order_line validated grain and types silver.customer_change ordered source history | v gold.fact_order_line one row per order line gold.dim_customer governed customer versions gold.sales_summary measures defined for reporting For the running example, Bronze retains the original event envelope so a parser or business-rule change can be replayed. Silver resolves duplicate delivery using the source key and log position, applies delete semantics, and quarantines malformed rows instead of silently dropping them. Gold performs the Type 2 lookup using the order’s event time and publishes the tested order-line fact. A gold layer can contain detailed facts as well as aggregates; “gold means aggregated” is a convention, not a data-model rule. Do not force every intermediate DataFrame into a permanent layer. Materialize a boundary when it supports replay, independent reuse, quality enforcement, ownership, or a measured workload. Otherwise, extra tables add storage, commits, metadata, orchestration, and schema contracts without adding a useful recovery point. The layering pattern is recommended in some lakehouse platforms, but it is not mandatory; choose boundaries that fit the system’s failure and consumption requirements. Test each transition independently. Bronze-to-silver should prove source positions are neither lost nor applied out of order. Silver should expose duplicate and rejected-row counts. Gold should prove fact grain, dimension coverage, Type 2 non-overlap, and reconciled measures. A single end-to-end row count cannot identify which boundary lost or multiplied records. 3.4 Schema evolution and data contracts In plain terms. A data contract is the promise a producer makes to its consumers: these columns, with these types and meanings, changed only by these rules. Schema evolution is how a table changes shape without breaking the people who read it. A schema contract is more than a list of field names. It should state field types, nullability, meaning, units, valid values, key semantics, event-time meaning, privacy classification, and compatibility expectations. Version the contract and identify an owner who can approve changes. Adding a nullable field is often compatible, depending on the consumer. Ask what null means for old rows, and which contract version adds the field. Renaming a field is not automatically compatible. Ask whether it is the same semantic field or a new definition, and provide a migration alias or a transition period. Widening a numeric type is often compatible if values keep their meaning. Ask whether the target engine supports the widening, and whether every producer can write it. Narrowing or reinterpreting a type is usually breaking. Plan the backfill, the validation, and the consumer migration. Changing a metric definition is semantically breaking even when the SQL type does not change. Version the metric or publish a new one, because schema compatibility cannot preserve meaning. Parquet readers may infer different schemas from different files. Spark supports schema merging, but it is disabled by default because collecting schemas across files has a cost. For table formats, schema and partition evolution are metadata operations with format-specific compatibility rules. Validate the logical contract before accepting either change. A contract can be as small as a reviewed YAML file next to the pipeline code. What matters is that each line is something a test can check: dataset: gold.fact_order_line owner: sales-data-team version: 2 grain: one row per product line on an accepted customer order primary_key: [order_id, line_number] columns: - {name: order_id, type: string, nullable: false} - {name: line_number, type: int, nullable: false} - {name: order_date_key, type: int, nullable: false} - {name: customer_sk, type: int, nullable: false, references: dim_customer.customer_sk, unknown_member: -1} - {name: product_sk, type: int, nullable: false, references: dim_product.product_sk, unknown_member: -1} - {name: net_amount, type: decimal(12,2), nullable: false, rule: gross_amount - discount_amount, currency: USD} compatibility: backward # add nullable columns only; renames need a new version freshness: loaded by 06:00 UTC daily 3.5 Hands-on: build the fact table end to end The example starts with curated order lines and customer change records. It derives end-exclusive customer validity ranges, resolves the customer version at order time, joins the product dimension, and creates one fact row per order line. It uses in-memory fixtures and local Spark; it does not write to the playground’s shared Hive or MinIO tables.
