Do not put every Hudi jar on the classpath. hudi-utilities-bundle registers a hudi data source as well as hudi-spark<N>-bundle, and both together fail the write with Multiple sources found for hudi. Hands-on: start and verify Prerequisites Requirement Detail Docker With Compose v2 (docker compose) Disk Free space in Docker’s VM for images and data: about 10 GB for core, 20 GB for all Memory 4 GB for the core profile, 10 GB for all. At idle they use about 1.9 GB and 6.3 to 7 GB; a Spark job adds 1 to 1.5 GB CPU The images are linux/amd64; Apple Silicon runs them under emulation Step 1: get the compose files git clone https://github.com/rangareddy/datalake-playground.git cd datalake-playground Step 2: start the stack SPARK_VERSION=3.5.9 sh run_datalake.sh start # core profile PROFILE=all SPARK_VERSION=3.5.9 sh run_datalake.sh start # adds Kafka, MySQL, Trino, Jupyter The first start pulls the images. Startup is ordered by health checks; expect a couple of minutes while Hive initialises its metastore schema. The start script defaults PLATFORM to linux/amd64 because that is what the images are built for. Setting it to linux/arm64 fails the pull with no matching manifest. sh run_datalake.sh status Every service should read Up (healthy), except the mc sidecar, which has no health check. The mc sidecar runs from ranga-minio and the notebook from ranga-spark, so those add no images of their own. The core profile is seven containers and was healthy 20 to 40 seconds after start. all is sixteen, with Kafka, and took 92 to 102 seconds; Kafka Connect is the slowest, because it scans every plugin jar before it opens its port. Step 3: check the Spark worker is registered Up (healthy) means a port answers. It does not mean the worker joined the master, and a job submitted to spark://spark-master:7077 without a worker waits forever: curl -s http://localhost:8080/json/ | python3 -c \ "import sys, json; print('alive workers:', json.load(sys.stdin)['aliveworkers'])" It should print alive workers: 1. If it prints 0, run docker restart spark-worker and check again. Step 4: check each table format lakehouse_check.py, in the root of the repo, has one function per format: check_iceberg, check_hudi and check_delta. Each writes three orders, updates one, and reads them back; cleanup then deletes everything the checks created. create_spark_session holds the catalog arrangement and extension order described above, so one session serves all three. docker cp lakehouse_check.py spark-master:/tmp/ docker exec spark-master bash -c '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit --master "local[2]" \ --driver-memory 1g \ --jars "$(ls $ICEBERG_HOME/*.jar $DELTA_HOME/*.jar $HUDI_HOME/hudi-spark*-bundle_*.jar \ | paste -sd, -)" \ /tmp/lakehouse_check.py' On the 3.5.9 line it printed: spark 3.5.9 PASS iceberg rows=3 shipped=1 PASS hudi rows=3 shipped=1 PASS delta rows=3 shipped=1 passed 3 of 3 On the 4.1.3 line the same three checks pass, with spark 4.1.3 on the first line. A passing run still prints a handful of warnings, such as NativeCodeLoader: Unable to load native-hadoop library and, from Hudi, Unable to attach Serviceability Agent. The repo’s README lists each one and why it is harmless. --driver-memory 1g is there on purpose; the failures section explains why. Step 5 (all profile): send records through Kafka The broker is kafka:29092 inside the network. A topic, three records and a read back: docker exec kafka kafka-topics --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 \ --create --topic orders --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1 printf '1001,PLACED
1002,PLACED
1003,SHIPPED
' | \ docker exec -i kafka kafka-console-producer --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 --topic orders docker exec kafka kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 \ --topic orders --from-beginning --max-messages 3 Created topic orders. 1001,PLACED 1002,PLACED 1003,SHIPPED Spark reads the same topic with spark.read.format("kafka") and kafka.bootstrap.servers=kafka:29092; the repo’s README has the full script. Kafka Connect’s REST API is on localhost:8083 and Kafka UI on localhost:9082. Step 6: run a post’s script Each post that uses the stack publishes its scripts in full. They all run the same way: copy the script into spark-master and submit it with the jars it needs, which are already in the image under $ICEBERG_HOME, $HUDI_HOME and $DELTA_HOME. docker cp time_travel_rollback.py spark-master:/tmp/ docker exec spark-master bash -c \ '$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-submit --master "local[2]" \ --jars $(ls $ICEBERG_HOME/iceberg-spark-runtime*.jar) /tmp/time_travel_rollback.py' That one is from time travel and rollback. Jupyter Lab (all profile) runs from the same Spark image at http://localhost:8888, with the same jars and environment. The numbers come out the same This is the part worth checking rather than trusting. The copy-on-write versus merge-on-read post measured its file accounting on Spark 4.1.3. The same measurement on the 3.5.9 line: == copy-on-write vs merge-on-read == copy-on-write before data=2f/4000r query returns 4000 copy-on-write after DELETE data=2f/3900r query returns 3900 snapshot ops ['append', 'overwrite'] merge-on-read before data=2f/4000r query returns 4000 merge-on-read after DELETE data=2f/4000r position-delete=1f/100r query returns 3900 snapshot ops ['append', 'delete'] Identical to the post. Copy-on-write rewrote to 3,900 records under an overwrite snapshot. Merge-on-read kept 4,000 records and added a 100-record delete file under a delete snapshot. Both queries return 3,900 rows. The claims are about Iceberg, not about one Spark build. Real-world scenarios and failures Each of these was found by running the stack, not by reading about it. The Spark worker was healthy and doing nothing. While re-verifying this post, the stack’s end-to-end test failed spark:worker-registered with expected ["aliveworkers":1]. The worker container read Up (healthy), and its JVM was running, but the master’s /json/ endpoint listed no workers. The custom images end with a keepalive loop, so container state says nothing about the service inside. The next check then submitted SparkPi to the cluster, and with no worker to run it, the job waited for resources indefinitely. Local-mode scripts (--master "local[2]") were unaffected, which is why everything else in this post still ran. docker restart spark-worker re-registered it in 15 seconds. Check the master before blaming a job: curl -s http://localhost:8080/json/ | python3 -c \ "import sys, json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['aliveworkers'])" Hudi’s first write is slow, and it looks like a hang. Creating a table and inserting into it for the first time bootstraps Hudi’s metadata table, which took about twenty seconds on a cold stack against MinIO. A smoke test run immediately after start read that as a failure; the same test passed on a second run with no change. Warm the table before timing anything. “It has no build that runs” is a conclusion worth re-testing. I wrote that about Hudi on Spark 4.1 and it was half right at best: it ran, it just could not merge, and the fix was a jar rather than a wait. The same note said Delta had no Scala 2.13 build past 4.0.0; 4.1.0 was on Maven Central. Version claims about someone else’s project go stale quietly. A full Docker disk does not announce itself. Seven unrelated checks failed at once: Hive could not create a temp directory and Spark’s S3A writes threw. The cause was the VM’s filesystem at 100%. Freeing 24 GB made every check pass on the next run. docker system df shows where the space went. A Spark script run on the host uses the host’s Spark. A format check run with spark-sql from a laptop’s PATH reported spark version 2.4.4, failed every check, and left a metastore_db/ and derby.log in the current directory. Spark scripts belong inside spark-master, through docker exec. Exit code 137 in the middle of a job is memory, not the job. The format check passed Iceberg and Hudi and then died with exit code 137, a SIGKILL, in two of five runs. The Docker VM had 7.8 GiB while running the full 16-container all profile, which wants 10 GB, and about 1.2 GB was available. The driver starts with the image’s spark.driver.memory 2g, and by the third connector the JVM outgrew what was left, so the kernel killed it. --driver-memory 1g fits what the check needs. Short of memory, a job can also just crawl: in one all-profile run the check took 17 minutes, where the next run took under 2. The real fix is giving Docker the memory the profile asks for. A restart can quietly drop half the stack. SPARK_VERSION=4.1.3 sh run_datalake.sh restart on a running all stack exited 0 and left seven containers: Kafka, MySQL, Trino and Jupyter were gone. restart works on the profile it is given, core by default, and docker compose down --remove-orphans removes every container that profile does not define. Pass the profile you started with: PROFILE=all SPARK_VERSION=4.1.3 sh run_datalake.sh restart. The first start logs a metastore connection failure, then recovers. On an empty data/, hive-metastore logged Connection to postgres:5432 refused and HiveMetaException: Failed to get schema version, then initialised its schema and came up healthy. Postgres runs its init SQL on a temporary server that listens only on a Unix socket, shuts it down, and opens TCP three seconds later. Its health check connects through the socket, so it passes during that window, and the metastore starts early. It happened in one of four first starts, and the metastore’s retry absorbed it every time. Optimisation, tuning and day-to-day operation Day-to-day commands Task Command Start sh run_datalake.sh start Stop, keeping data sh run_datalake.sh stop Status sh run_datalake.sh status Follow logs sh run_datalake.sh logs spark-master Check a compose edit sh run_datalake.sh validate Switch Spark line PROFILE=all SPARK_VERSION=4.1.3 sh run_datalake.sh restart (drop PROFILE=all on core) Shell into Spark docker exec -it spark-master bash stop does a down without -v, so the Postgres data directory and the MinIO object store under data/ survive. For a clean slate: sh run_datalake.sh stop rm -rf data logs sh run_datalake.sh start Configuration lives in two places Service wiring, ports and the MinIO credentials are in the compose files, and the start script reads three optional variables: PROFILE (core or all), SPARK_VERSION and PLATFORM. Engine configuration, spark-defaults.conf, core-site.xml, hive-site.xml and the Trino catalogs, is baked into the images. Editing a compose value takes effect on restart; changing engine configuration means passing --conf to your job instead. Checklist Give Docker 4 GB of memory and 10 GB of disk for core, 10 GB and 20 GB for all. Leave PLATFORM at linux/amd64; the images are built for it. Check aliveworkers on the master’s /json/ endpoint before submitting to the cluster. Run lakehouse_check.py after the first start. Run Spark scripts inside spark-master, not on the host. List Delta’s session extension before Iceberg’s when a session uses both. Warm a new Hudi table before timing it. Create your own tables under a namespace no post uses, and drop them with PURGE afterwards. Summary and key takeaways The stack is a single node with one writer. It will not show you concurrent writers at scale, S3 throttling, cross-region latency, or anything about IAM, because MinIO has none of them. The Spark-internals measurements in shuffle internals and performance tuning were taken against a plain Spark container, because they are about the engine rather than the lakehouse around it. What it does give you is a correct, reproducible environment for table-format behaviour, which is where most of the surprises live. Clone and start. The public repo is the compose files and a start script, and the pinned images are pulled once. One variable picks the Spark line, and everything version-coupled follows from it. All three formats share one session only with Delta on spark_catalog, Iceberg on a named catalog, Hudi by path, and Delta’s extension listed first. Up (healthy) is not a test. Check the worker count and run lakehouse_check.py before trusting the stack. References datalake-playground, the compose files, start script and lakehouse_check.py Apache Iceberg Spark procedures for the calls the demos make Apache Hudi Spark guide for the table properties Hudi requires Delta Lake quick start for the DeltaCatalog session configuration Docker Compose environment for inline service variables Trademarks Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, Apache Kafka, Apache Hive, Apache and the Apache feather logo are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries. Delta Lake is a trademark of the Linux Foundation. Trino is a trademark of the Trino Software Foundation. MinIO is a trademark of MinIO, Inc. Docker is a trademark of Docker, Inc.

entry.title: What Hive tables could not do, and why Iceberg exists

link.title: What Hive tables could not do, and why Iceberg exists

entry.content:
• The Hive table is a directory
  • What Iceberg changes
  • The consequences, measured
    • Atomic commits and history
    • Schema changes that touch no data
    • Partition layout that can change
  • Seeing the difference in one session
  • The failure modes it removes
  • What it costs to adopt
  • What you give up
  • When the older design is still right
  • A model worth keeping
  • References
  • Trademarks

TL;DR

  • A Hive table is a directory, and the files in it. Planning means listing directories, so cost grows with partition count and correctness depends on the filesystem.
  • An Iceberg table is a list of files recorded in metadata. Planning reads metadata, never lists a directory, and a commit is one atomic pointer swap.
  • That single change is what makes atomic writes, time travel, schema evolution and partition evolution possible — they are consequences of file tracking, not separate features.
  • Schema changes are metadata-only: renaming a column left the underlying data files untouched and kept its field id, 4.
  • Partition layout can change without rewriting history. After switching months(ts) to days(ts), existing files kept spec_id = 0 and stayed queryable.

The Hive table is a directory

For a decade the answer to “what is a table on a data lake” was: a directory, plus a row in a metastore saying where that directory is and what columns to expect.

s3://warehouse/trips/
├── dt=2026-01-05/  part-00000.parquet  part-00001.parquet
├── dt=2026-01-06/  part-00000.parquet
└── dt=2026-01-07/  part-00000.parquet

Everything good about that design comes from its simplicity: any engine that can list a path and read Parquet can read the table. Everything bad comes from the same place — the set of files in the table is whatever happens to be in the directory right now.

Four consequences follow, and every one of them is a production problem.

Planning means listing. To find what to read, the engine lists directories. A table with 50,000 partitions costs 50,000 listings before a single row is read. On object storage, where listing is an API call with latency and rate limits, this dominates query time on exactly the tables that are big enough to matter.

A write is not atomic. Writing a partition means putting files into a directory. A reader that lists mid-write sees a partial result. There is no moment at which the table changes from the old state to the new one; there is a period during which it is neither.

There is no history. Overwriting a partition deletes the previous files. If the job that produced them was wrong, the previous data is gone. Recovery means restoring from a backup you hopefully took.

Schema is a convention. The metastore records column names and positions. The Parquet files record their own. When these disagree — because someone added a column, or reordered one — you get wrong values rather than an error, because matching is by name or position and both are fragile.

What Iceberg changes

Iceberg replaces “the files in this directory” with “the files this metadata says are in the table”. That is the whole idea, and everything else is a consequence.

flowchart TB
    C[Catalog] -->|"points at the current"| M["metadata.json<br/>schema, partition specs, snapshots"]
    M -->|"current snapshot"| ML["manifest list<br/>snap-*.avro"]
    ML -->|"manifests, with partition ranges"| MF["manifest files<br/>*.avro"]
    MF -->|"data files, with column bounds"| D["*.parquet"]

The catalog holds one pointer: which metadata file is current. A commit writes new metadata and swaps that pointer atomically. The swap is the commit — before it, readers see the old table; after it, the new one; never anything in between.

Because the metadata names every file, planning never lists a directory. It reads the manifest list, discards manifests whose partition ranges cannot match, reads the surviving manifests, and discards files whose column bounds cannot match. Cost scales with metadata size, which you control, rather than with partition count, which you do not.

The consequences, measured

These are not separate features bolted on. Each one falls out of tracking files in metadata.

Atomic commits and history

Every commit writes a new metadata file rather than editing the old one. A table created and appended to three times accumulates them predictably:

after CREATE, before any data   metadata_files=2    data_files=0
after append #1                 metadata_files=5    data_files=1
after append #2                 metadata_files=8    data_files=2
after append #3                 metadata_files=11   data_files=3

Three metadata files per commit: a manifest, a manifest list, and a new metadata.json. Old snapshots stay valid because their metadata still exists and still names its files, which is exactly what time travel reads.

Schema changes that touch no data

Adding a column, renaming one and changing a type, on a table holding 9,000 rows:

before: ['id', 'event_ts', 'region', 'amount']
after : ['id', 'event_ts', 'region', 'amount_usd', 'currency']
rows still readable                = 9000
old rows have NULL currency        = 9000
data files after schema change     = 3   (unchanged: nothing was rewritten)

Three data files before, three after. The rename was a metadata edit. It is safe because Iceberg identifies columns by field id, not by name or position:

field id=1   name=id           type=long
field id=2   name=event_ts     type=timestamptz
field id=3   name=region       type=string
field id=4   name=amount_usd   type=double
field id=5   name=currency     type=string

amount became amount_usd and kept id 4. The Parquet files still record field 4; the schema now calls it something else. This is the fix for the Hive failure where a rename silently reads the wrong column.

Partition layout that can change

A table partitioned by month, switched to day, then appended to:

partition-specs: [{"spec-id": 0, ... "transform": "month", "source-id": 2},
                  {"spec-id": 1, ... "transform": "day",   "source-id": 2}]
default-spec-id: 1
spec_id per data file: [1, 0, 0]

Two files still carry spec_id = 0. Nothing was rewritten, both layouts coexist on disk, and all rows stay queryable through one table. In a Hive table the partition layout is the directory structure, so changing it means moving every file.

Partitioning is also hidden: the query names the real column and Iceberg applies the transform.

SELECT count(*) FROM local.db.events
WHERE event_ts >= timestamp'2026-01-06 00:00:00'
  AND event_ts <  timestamp'2026-01-07 00:00:00'

That returned 3,000 rows without naming a partition column, while the files sat in event_ts_day=2026-01-06. The Hive equivalent requires the user to know the physical column and filter on it, and silently scans everything when they forget.

Seeing the difference in one session

The argument is short enough to run. Both tables hold the same rows; only the format differs.

# Hive-style: a directory of Parquet, partitioned physically
(df.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("region")
   .format("parquet").saveAsTable("legacy_events"))

# Iceberg: the same data, tracked in metadata
spark.sql("""
    CREATE TABLE local.db.events (id BIGINT, event_ts TIMESTAMP, region STRING, amount DOUBLE)
    USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(event_ts))""")
df.writeTo("local.db.events").append()

Now ask each one a question only the Iceberg table can answer:

-- what did this table look like an hour ago?
SELECT count(*) FROM local.db.events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-01-06 09:00:00';

-- which files does it consist of, and how big are they?
SELECT count(*), round(avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1048576, 1) FROM local.db.events.files;

-- what has been done to it, and by which commit?
SELECT snapshot_id, operation, summary['added-records'] FROM local.db.events.snapshots;

There is no equivalent for the Hive table, and that is the whole difference stated as a capability rather than an argument: the Iceberg table knows what it is made of.

The failure modes it removes

Four concrete situations, each routine on a directory-based table.

A reader sees a half-written partition. A job overwrites dt=2026-01-06 by deleting and rewriting files; a query running at that moment reads whatever exists. On Iceberg the query resolved a snapshot before the write began and is unaffected.

Two writers both “succeed”. Two jobs write to the same partition concurrently and the result is the union, the last one, or a mixture, depending on timing. On Iceberg one commit wins the compare-and-swap and the other retries against the new state.

A rename silently empties a column. A column renamed in the metastore no longer matches old files, and historical rows read NULL. On Iceberg the files record field ids, so a rename is a label change.

A backfill has to be undone. On a directory table, the previous files are gone. On Iceberg:

CALL local.system.rollback_to_snapshot('db.events', 9044140986145286505);

Each of these is silent on the older design. None produces an error; all produce wrong answers or unrecoverable states, which is why they are expensive to find.

What it costs to adopt

Being fair about the other side of the ledger.

Three jobs you did not have before. Compaction, delete-file compaction and snapshot expiry. None is optional on a table under real write traffic, and a table that skips them degrades in ways a Hive table does not.

A catalog to operate. Something must own the pointer and swap it atomically. That is a service to deploy, secure, monitor and back up — infrastructure a directory never needed.

Reader compatibility becomes a constraint. Every engine touching the table must understand the metadata tree, and the format version becomes a contract across teams.

Metadata grows with commits, not data. A low-volume table committing every minute develops a metadata problem a high-volume daily batch table never will, which inverts the intuition most people bring.

What you give up

Iceberg is not free, and pretending otherwise sets people up for surprises.

Metadata is a thing you now operate. Every commit writes files. Streaming writes accumulate them quickly, and tables need compaction, snapshot expiry and occasionally manifest rewriting on a schedule.

Every engine needs Iceberg support. A Hive table can be read by anything that lists a directory. An Iceberg table needs a reader that understands the metadata tree. That is broadly true now — Spark, Trino, Flink, Dremio, Snowflake, BigQuery — but “broadly” is not “universally”, and a legacy tool doing directory listings will see nothing useful.

The catalog becomes infrastructure. Something has to own the pointer swap atomically. That is a service to run, secure and back up.

Small tables gain little. A table of a few files, written once daily, read by one engine, has none of the problems Iceberg solves. The metadata overhead is real and the benefit is not.

When the older design is still right

A table written once and read as a whole, small enough that listing is instant, consumed by one engine, with no update or delete requirement and no need for history — that is a directory of Parquet files, and adding a table format to it buys complexity rather than capability.

The moment any of those stops being true — concurrent writers, row-level deletes, a schema that changes, an auditor asking what the table said last Tuesday, or a partition count where listing hurts — the directory stops being enough, and the reason is always the same: nothing is tracking which files belong to the table.

A model worth keeping

A Hive table says “the data is over there”. An Iceberg table says “these exact files, with this schema, as of this snapshot”.

Every Iceberg feature people list separately — ACID, time travel, schema evolution, partition evolution, hidden partitioning — is that one sentence applied to a different problem. Which is also why they compose: they are not features, they are consequences.

References

  • Iceberg table specification for the metadata tree and its guarantees
  • Iceberg documentation for the engine and catalog support matrix
  • Apache Iceberg architecture for the metadata tree in depth
  • Open table formats in practice for how Iceberg, Hudi and Delta differ
  • A local Iceberg playground for an environment to try this in

Trademarks

Apache Iceberg, Apache Hive, Apache Spark, Apache Parquet, Apache and the Apache feather logo are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries.

The Hive equivalent requires the user to know the physical column and filter on it, and silently scans everything when they forget. Seeing the difference in one session The argument is short enough to run. Both tables hold the same rows; only the format differs. # Hive-style: a directory of Parquet, partitioned physically (df.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("region") .format("parquet").saveAsTable("legacy_events")) # Iceberg: the same data, tracked in metadata spark.sql(""" CREATE TABLE local.db.events (id BIGINT, event_ts TIMESTAMP, region STRING, amount DOUBLE) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(event_ts))""") df.writeTo("local.db.events").append() Now ask each one a question only the Iceberg table can answer: -- what did this table look like an hour ago? SELECT count(*) FROM local.db.events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-01-06 09:00:00'; -- which files does it consist of, and how big are they? SELECT count(*), round(avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1048576, 1) FROM local.db.events.files; -- what has been done to it, and by which commit? SELECT snapshot_id, operation, summary['added-records'] FROM local.db.events.snapshots; There is no equivalent for the Hive table, and that is the whole difference stated as a capability rather than an argument: the Iceberg table knows what it is made of. The failure modes it removes Four concrete situations, each routine on a directory-based table. A reader sees a half-written partition. A job overwrites dt=2026-01-06 by deleting and rewriting files; a query running at that moment reads whatever exists. On Iceberg the query resolved a snapshot before the write began and is unaffected. Two writers both “succeed”. Two jobs write to the same partition concurrently and the result is the union, the last one, or a mixture, depending on timing. On Iceberg one commit wins the compare-and-swap and the other retries against the new state. A rename silently empties a column. A column renamed in the metastore no longer matches old files, and historical rows read NULL. On Iceberg the files record field ids, so a rename is a label change. A backfill has to be undone. On a directory table, the previous files are gone. On Iceberg: CALL local.system.rollback_to_snapshot('db.events', 9044140986145286505); Each of these is silent on the older design. None produces an error; all produce wrong answers or unrecoverable states, which is why they are expensive to find. What it costs to adopt Being fair about the other side of the ledger. Three jobs you did not have before. Compaction, delete-file compaction and snapshot expiry. None is optional on a table under real write traffic, and a table that skips them degrades in ways a Hive table does not. A catalog to operate. Something must own the pointer and swap it atomically. That is a service to deploy, secure, monitor and back up — infrastructure a directory never needed. Reader compatibility becomes a constraint. Every engine touching the table must understand the metadata tree, and the format version becomes a contract across teams. Metadata grows with commits, not data. A low-volume table committing every minute develops a metadata problem a high-volume daily batch table never will, which inverts the intuition most people bring. What you give up Iceberg is not free, and pretending otherwise sets people up for surprises. Metadata is a thing you now operate. Every commit writes files. Streaming writes accumulate them quickly, and tables need compaction, snapshot expiry and occasionally manifest rewriting on a schedule. Every engine needs Iceberg support. A Hive table can be read by anything that lists a directory. An Iceberg table needs a reader that understands the metadata tree. That is broadly true now — Spark, Trino, Flink, Dremio, Snowflake, BigQuery — but “broadly” is not “universally”, and a legacy tool doing directory listings will see nothing useful. The catalog becomes infrastructure. Something has to own the pointer swap atomically. That is a service to run, secure and back up. Small tables gain little. A table of a few files, written once daily, read by one engine, has none of the problems Iceberg solves. The metadata overhead is real and the benefit is not. When the older design is still right A table written once and read as a whole, small enough that listing is instant, consumed by one engine, with no update or delete requirement and no need for history — that is a directory of Parquet files, and adding a table format to it buys complexity rather than capability. The moment any of those stops being true — concurrent writers, row-level deletes, a schema that changes, an auditor asking what the table said last Tuesday, or a partition count where listing hurts — the directory stops being enough, and the reason is always the same: nothing is tracking which files belong to the table. A model worth keeping A Hive table says “the data is over there”. An Iceberg table says “these exact files, with this schema, as of this snapshot”. Every Iceberg feature people list separately — ACID, time travel, schema evolution, partition evolution, hidden partitioning — is that one sentence applied to a different problem. Which is also why they compose: they are not features, they are consequences.
